q-kadikoy.name: Kadıköy
q-kadikoy.teaser: The shore the ancients called blind, and the side of the water Istanbul now crosses to for dinner
q-kadikoy.story: Megarian settlers founded Chalcedon on this headland some seventeen years before Byzantium went up across the water, and the ancients never let them forget it. Herodotus has a Persian general call them blind for missing the better site; later writers turned the jibe into a verdict of Apollo's oracle. After the conquest Mehmed II gave the farmland to Hızır Bey, the city's first Ottoman judge, and Chalcedon became Kadıköy, the judge's village. The joke has aged badly. Çiya cooks its regional pots beside the market, Araf holds a MICHELIN star further out in the district, and on Saturday nights the European side takes the ferry over to eat.
q-kadikoy.why: Come in by water: the market streets, told in the larder, start five minutes from the pier.
facts: The market streets by day and Kadife Sokak's bars at night
Saturday, from the afternoon market into the evening
The Eminönü ferry in, told under walks
Çiya Sofrası by the market; Araf İstanbul if you can win a seat

q-moda.name: Moda
q-moda.teaser: Wooden villas built by three communities, and a 1917 pier that now lends out books
q-moda.story: Moda is the headland below Kadıköy, laid out in the late nineteenth century when Greek, Armenian and Levantine families built wooden summer houses down the lanes to the water. Their churches, Hagia Triada among them, still hold services for congregations that are a fraction of what they were. The ferry pier, designed by Vedat Tek and dated to about 1917, sat shut for years after a botched restoration; the city reopened it in August 2022 with a book café and a public library inside. The lanes still run downhill to the sea, and so does the whole district at the end of the day.
q-moda.why: Take a book to the pier library and read with the strait outside the window.
facts: The old villas, the community churches and the restored pier
The coast path round the point, told under walks
WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas on Ferit Tek Sokak

q-yeldegirmeni.name: Yeldeğirmeni
q-yeldegirmeni.teaser: Windmills once, then the first apartment blocks on this shore, now murals on every gable wall
q-yeldegirmeni.story: The name means windmill, for the flour mills that once ground grain for the palace on this rise between the Kadıköy pier and Haydarpaşa. Armenians, Greeks and Jews settled here from the fifteenth century; a handful of their families remain. It was the first quarter in Kadıköy to put up apartment blocks instead of wooden houses, and several of those early blocks still stand on their original streets. About a decade ago a mural programme covered the blank gable walls with large paintings, and small coffee rooms and quieter bars followed. It is the morning half of Kadıköy: residential, low and best enjoyed with your head tilted back.
q-yeldegirmeni.why: Walk it before noon, when the light falls on the painted walls and the streets are still yours.
facts: The murals and the first apartment blocks on the Asian shore
The painted gable walls, looked at from the street corners

q-uskudar.name: Üsküdar
q-uskudar.teaser: The golden city of the Greeks, and the shore where the sultan's caravan set out for Mecca
q-uskudar.story: Megarian settlers came here too, and called the place Chrysopolis, the golden city. Ottoman Üsküdar was the terminus of the Anatolian caravan routes and, for much of the empire's life, the shore from which the Surre caravan left carrying the sultan's gifts to Mecca; the regular caravan ended in 1915. That history made Üsküdar Muslim, settled and sober while the far shore was mixed and licensed, and it still shows at the table. The lokantas here, with their steam trays of stews and pilafs at noon, are some of the best in the city, and the meyhanes are essentially absent.
q-uskudar.why: Eat lunch here, not dinner: this shore puts its best cooking into the noon steam tray.
facts: Ottoman mosques, lokanta lunches and the Asian waterfront
The dusk crossing back west, told under walks
A steam-tray lokanta lunch; there is barely a meyhane here

q-kuzguncuk.name: Kuzguncuk
q-kuzguncuk.teaser: A mosque, a synagogue and churches on one short street, in a village of wooden houses
q-kuzguncuk.story: Kuzguncuk was once a largely Jewish village on the Asian shore, one stop north of Üsküdar, and its wooden houses still climb the slope behind the water. On İcadiye Caddesi you pass a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue of 1878, an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones, close enough together to see from one doorway to the next. Almost none of those congregations still live here. It is the plainest physical proof of the mixed city this guide keeps describing, and the walk up the street, told under walks, takes barely an hour.
q-kuzguncuk.why: Come on a Sunday afternoon, when the village is at home and the street is at its gentlest.
facts: Wooden houses and three faiths' buildings on one street
Late afternoon, best on a Sunday
The İcadiye Caddesi walk, told under walks

q-pera.name: Beyoğlu / Pera
q-pera.teaser: The avenue was called the Grand Rue de Péra, and for most of its life it was not Turkish
q-pera.story: Pera is Greek for beyond: the quarter across the Golden Horn from the old city. Foreigners won the right to buy property in the empire in 1867 and spent it here, building the Grand Rue de Péra into a street of arcades, apartment houses and hotels in every style the century could supply. The Cité de Péra of 1876 became the Çiçek Pasajı, its elegant shops turned into rough meyhanes with barrels for tables. The avenue is İstiklal Caddesi now, running from Taksim down to Tünel, and the evening gathers at its lower end, in the lanes of Asmalımescit and Nevizade, where the rakı comes out with the meze.
q-pera.why: Save a Thursday night for the lanes at the bottom of İstiklal, when the meyhanes fill.
facts: Nineteenth-century arcades and the meyhane lanes
The Çiçek Pasajı, the 1876 Cité de Péra
Asmalı Cavit, on Asmalı Mescit Caddesi

q-cihangir.name: Cihangir
q-cihangir.teaser: A dead prince's mosque, then the writers and the cats, now a handful of small serious kitchens
q-cihangir.story: The quarter is named for the mosque Sinan built in 1559 for Şehzade Cihangir, Süleyman's son, dead at twenty-two; the building on the hilltop now is an 1889 replacement after repeated fires and earthquakes. The slope below Taksim became the writers-and-cats quarter in the 1990s and has held that register better than most gentrified districts manage: café tables on steep pavements, bookshops, cats asleep on parked cars. Casius cooks Antakya food here from a stone oven and carries a 2026 Bib Gourmand, and Van Kahvaltı Evi lays out the eastern breakfast a few streets away.
q-cihangir.why: Climb to the mosque terrace in the afternoon for the view straight down over the Bosphorus mouth.
facts: Steep lanes, cafés and two serious tables
The Cihangir mosque terrace over the water
Casius Antioch Kitchen for dinner; Van Kahvaltı Evi for breakfast

q-nisantasi.name: Nişantaşı
q-nisantasi.teaser: Named for the stones that recorded how far a sultan's arrow flew
q-nisantasi.story: A nişan taşı is an inscribed stone recording a record shot, and this was the sultans' archery ground: Selim III's stone here dates from 1790–91, Mahmud II's from 1811. Mahmud II then encouraged people to settle the field, and the archery ground became the city's grandest residential grid, with Teşvikiye running on next door. It has never been a cooking quarter. Come instead for the evening register: the wine bars and listening rooms on the side streets, the shopping avenues lit up after dark, and the sense of the Republic's comfortable middle class at home.
q-nisantasi.why: Treat it as an evening walk and a glass, not a dinner: the kitchens worth crossing for are elsewhere.
facts: The old archery ground's grid of streets and its wine bars

q-karakoy.name: Karaköy and Galata
q-karakoy.teaser: A Genoese city-state with its own walls, and a banker's staircase down to the cruise front
q-karakoy.story: Galata was a colony of the Republic of Genoa from 1267 to 1453: walled, self-governing and crowned by the tower it finished in 1348. Five centuries later the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo cut his baroque double staircase down to Bankalar Caddesi so he could walk from his house to his bank, and the steps still curl down the hill. Galataport reopened this waterfront to the public in 2021, and the cruise ships now tie up below the old banks. Neolokal holds a MICHELIN star on the top floor of SALT Galata, the former Ottoman Bank; the roof bars round about hold the view.
q-karakoy.why: Be on a Galata roof at sundown, when the old city's domes go black against the sky.
facts: Genoese Galata, the bank street and the open waterfront
The Camondo stairs off Bankalar Caddesi
Neolokal in SALT Galata; Karaköy Güllüoğlu for baklava

q-balat-fener.name: Balat and Fener
q-balat-fener.teaser: Jewish Balat and Greek Fener side by side on the Golden Horn, and a red school above both
q-balat-fener.story: Two neighbouring quarters share one stretch of the Golden Horn and two different pasts. Balat is probably named from palation, palace, for the Blachernae ruins on the hill, and for five centuries it was home to Sephardic and Romaniote Jews. Fener is Phanar, the lighthouse, which in turn named the Phanariots, the Greek families who supplied the Ottoman state with its interpreters and Danubian princes. Above both rises the Red Castle, the Greek college built in 1881–83 by Konstantinos Dimadis at a recorded 17,210 Ottoman gold pounds, for a school that opened in 1454. It has outlasted the community it was built to teach.
q-balat-fener.why: Walk the lanes before ten, then come back after dark for dinner at Agora Meyhanesi.
facts: Synagogues, the Patriarchate and steep lanes of old houses
Before 10:00 for the lanes; evening for dinner
Ahrida and the Patriarchate, both told under walks
Agora Meyhanesi, trading since 1890, on Mürselpaşa Caddesi

q-arnavutkoy.name: Arnavutköy
q-arnavutkoy.teaser: The fastest water on the strait, an Albanian name, and a scented strawberry that lost its fields
q-arnavutkoy.story: The Byzantines called this bank Mega Revma, the great current, for the water that runs fastest along it. Mehmed II resettled Albanians here in 1468 and the Turkish name followed, but the village stayed heavily Greek into the twentieth century, with Armenian and Jewish families beside them. Its hillsides grew the Ottoman strawberry, small, less sweet than the modern berry and intensely scented, on forty hectares that are streets now. What survives on the water is the best row of bay-windowed wooden yalı on the European shore, standing with their feet in the current. Tam Ocakbaşı keeps an Adana fire going a few doors back.
q-arnavutkoy.why: Stand on the quay and watch the current pull the boats sideways: it is the reason for the name.
facts: The wooden yalı row and the fast water in front of it
The shore walk north to Bebek, told under walks
Tam Ocakbaşı; book ahead for Friday and Saturday

q-bebek.name: Bebek
q-bebek.teaser: The calmest bay on the European shore, and a khedive's palace demoted to a consulate
q-bebek.story: Bebek is Turkish for baby, and its bay is the calmest water on the European shore, which is why the yalı around it belong to people who can afford calm. The white art nouveau pile on the front was built in 1899–1901 for Emine Valide Pasha, mother of the last Khedive of Egypt. It became the Egyptian embassy and was later downgraded to a consulate once the Republic moved its capital to Ankara and the embassies followed. The whole city's demotion sits in one building. In the evening the bay fills with moored boats, the promenade fills with strollers, and the lights come on along the far shore.
q-bebek.why: Arrive on foot from Arnavutköy at sundown and finish on the bay wall with the lights coming on.
facts: The bay, the yalı and the Egyptian consulate
The art nouveau consulate on the waterfront

q-tarabya.name: Tarabya
q-tarabya.teaser: Poison, renamed cure, then rented out to the ambassadors for the summer
q-tarabya.story: The Byzantines called the bay Pharmakia, poison, after the Medea legend, until it was renamed Therapeia, the cure, for its springs; tradition credits Archbishop Atticus with the change, some time between 406 and 425. Later it became the summer address of the embassies, escaping the city heat on the cooler upper strait. Abdülhamid II gave the Germans their plot in 1880; the residence went up between 1885 and 1887 and has run since 2011 as an artists' residency. The bay below is a long row of fish restaurants, lit up at night with the boats moored in front.
q-tarabya.why: Come for a fish dinner on the bay after dark, when the restaurant lights double in the water.
facts: The fish-restaurant row on the bay
The German summer residence grounds, seen from the road
Fish on the bay; choose it off the ice and agree the price first

w-kadikoy-ferry.name: The vapur: Eminönü to Kadıköy
w-kadikoy-ferry.teaser: The best room in Istanbul moves, costs a commuter fare and serves tea on deck
w-kadikoy-ferry.story: Şirket-i Hayriye, the Ottoman empire's first joint-stock company, began running boats across the strait in 1851, and until the first Bosphorus bridge opened in 1973 the water was the only way over. The boats are municipal now, run by Şehir Hatları since 2006: some 30 vessels on 32 lines between 53 piers, carrying 40 million passengers in 2023. Take the open deck. Tea comes round in tulip glasses on a tray that never spills, gulls track the stern for thrown simit, and the old city slides apart from Galata as you pull out. It is transport, not a tour, which is exactly why it works.
w-kadikoy-ferry.why: Ride it at dusk once: both shores light up and the crossing feels like the whole city at once.
facts: Open deck or saloon; no ticket queue with a card
Tea in a tulip glass from the deck tray

w-uskudar-ferry.name: Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar
w-uskudar-ferry.teaser: The shortest hop to Asia: go over in daylight and come back west into the sunset
w-uskudar-ferry.story: This is the quickest crossing to Asia, and the view does the work. Offshore stands the Maiden's Tower, on a rock the Athenians had already used as a customs post; there was a Byzantine tower here by 1110, rebuilt many times since, and what you see is Ottoman. On landing, Sinan's Mihrimah Sultan mosque rises right above the Üsküdar pier, and his small Şemsi Paşa mosque sits a few minutes south, almost in the water. Walk the shore, then catch a boat back westward as the light goes, with the European skyline lighting up dome by dome in front of you.
w-uskudar-ferry.why: Time the return for sunset: the old city's skyline comes up in silhouette dead ahead.
facts: Ferry deck, then the level Üsküdar shore
Şemsi Paşa mosque at the water's edge

w-golden-horn-line.name: The Golden Horn line: Üsküdar to Eyüpsultan
w-golden-horn-line.teaser: One boat, nine piers, and the front door of every Golden Horn walk in this guide
w-golden-horn-line.story: The Haliç line calls at Üsküdar, Karaköy, Kasımpaşa, Fener, Balat, Hasköy, Ayvansaray, Sütlüce and Eyüpsultan, which means it stops at the front door of every walk in the next group. The Golden Horn is 7.5 kilometres long and was an industrial sewer within living memory; the clean-up through the 1980s and 1990s is the reason you can sit on deck now and enjoy the smell of the water. Watch the shipyards at Hasköy, the domes of Fener and the cemetery hill at the top slide past. Ride to the end, walk back down a pier or two, and take the boat home.
w-golden-horn-line.why: Use it as the thread for a whole Golden Horn day: one fare, hop off, hop on again.
facts: Morning, to leave time for the walks
Getting off at Fener or Balat
An İstanbulkart; same fare as other ferries

w-arnavutkoy-bebek.name: Arnavutköy to Bebek
w-arnavutkoy-bebek.teaser: Painted timber houses standing in the water, then a bay full of boats at the end
w-arnavutkoy-bebek.story: Start at Arnavutköy pier and walk north on the shore road, with the strait at your elbow and the current running hard beside the wall. The painted timber houses along the water date from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many with art nouveau fronts, and they stand straight out of the sea. Fishermen line the railing, tankers slide past close enough to read their names, and the road bends round to open the bay at Bebek, full of moored boats. Pass the Egyptian consulate, told in the Bebek card, and stop on the bay wall for tea.
w-arnavutkoy-bebek.why: Walk it northward late in the day so the light is on the houses and the bay waits at the end.
facts: About 1.5–3 km one way; sources differ
About an hour at strolling pace
Flat pavement along the shore road; no shade at midday
The yalı fronts just north of Arnavutköy pier

w-kuzguncuk.name: Kuzguncuk's one street
w-kuzguncuk.teaser: A mosque, a synagogue and churches on one short road, and a gravestone from 1562
w-kuzguncuk.story: İcadiye Caddesi runs a few hundred metres up from the water, and the walk is simply up it and back. Sephardic Jews settled here after the expulsions from Spain; the oldest Jewish gravestone in the neighbourhood is dated 1562. The Bet Yaakov synagogue is conventionally dated 1878 and is probably older. Around it stand a mosque and the Armenian and Greek churches. The community thinned after 1948 and emptied fast after the 1955 pogrom, and migrants from the Black Sea coast moved into the wooden houses. One street holds the whole argument, and residents still live in it.
w-kuzguncuk.why: Walk it slowly on a Sunday and keep your voice down: this is a lived-in street, not a set.
facts: Kuzguncuk pier, or a short bus north from Üsküdar
A few hundred metres up and back
Gentle climb on a residential street
Bet Yaakov synagogue near the waterfront end

w-moda.name: Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk
w-moda.teaser: The flat seafront the Asian side actually uses, pointed straight at the sunset
w-moda.story: From Kadıköy pier, walk south along the shore with the yachts of the marina on one side and the joggers on the other. From the 1870s this was a summer address for the city's minorities, which is why Greek Orthodox, Anglican and Catholic churches and the Lycée Saint-Joseph of 1870 still stand among the apartment blocks above you. Pass the restored pier, told in the Moda card, and keep going out to Moda Burnu. There, sit on the grass with half of Kadıköy and watch the sun drop behind the domes of the old city across the water.
w-moda.why: Be on the grass at Moda Burnu before sunset; the whole Asian side comes to watch it.
facts: Kadıköy pier, heading south along the shore
About 1 hour with a sit on the point
The grass at Moda Burnu facing the old city
Something to sit on; the nostalgia tram loops back to Kadıköy

w-fener.name: Fener: the Patriarchate and the iron church
w-fener.teaser: Orthodoxy's senior see behind an iron gate, then a whole church cast in Vienna
w-fener.story: Get off at Fener pier and climb to the Ecumenical Patriarchate, here since about 1600; St George's Cathedral inside is free, with modest dress. Between 1711 and 1821 the Phanariot Greeks of these streets governed Wallachia and Moldavia for the sultans. Above, the Red Castle college now has almost no pupils. Nearby, St Mary of the Mongols is the only Byzantine church in the city never to have stopped serving Greek Orthodox worship, with the firmans of Mehmed II and Bayezid II still hanging inside. Finish on the shore road at St Stephen's, the Bulgarian church cast in Vienna and consecrated on 8 September 1898.
w-fener.why: Touch the walls of St Stephen's: some 500 tonnes of iron, bolted together on soft ground.
facts: Fener pier on the Haliç line
Steep lanes up to the Patriarchate, flat shore road back
St Stephen's iron church on Mürselpaşa Caddesi
Covered shoulders and knees for the churches

w-balat.name: Balat: Ahrida and the Jewish quarter
w-balat.teaser: Eighteen synagogues once, three still working, and one with a bimah shaped like a ship's prow
w-balat.story: Bayezid II opened the city to Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition after 1492, and Balat became the centre of Istanbul's Jewish life, with eighteen synagogues at its height. Ahrida was founded in the fifteenth century by Jews from Ohrid, and its wooden bimah is built like a boat's prow. By tradition Sabbatai Zevi prayed here, the self-proclaimed Messiah of Smyrna, arrested on reaching Constantinople in February 1666. Three synagogues still work. Balat itself is now overwhelmingly Muslim and, in the 2020s, heavily gentrified, so walk the steep streets early, before the photographers arrive.
w-balat.why: Arrange the Ahrida visit days ahead: there is no walk-in, and the prow bimah is the reason to come.
facts: Written permission arranged in advance through the Chief Rabbinate, and ID

w-eyup.name: Eyüpsultan and the hill above it
w-eyup.teaser: A pilgrimage mosque, a cemetery climbing the slope, and a cable car to the view
w-eyup.story: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, a companion of the Prophet, died during the Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s. His tomb was declared rediscovered after 1453, and the mosque raised over it became the place where each new sultan was girded with the Sword of Osman. It is still a working pilgrimage site: families in their best clothes, boys in white satin before their circumcision, pigeons on the courtyard stones. Dress for it and avoid Friday midday. Then climb through the cemetery, or take the cable car, to the Pierre Loti café, which has its own card among the rooms to linger.
w-eyup.why: Walk up through the cemetery rather than ride: the headstones are the best history lesson on the hill.
facts: Eyüpsultan pier at the head of the Golden Horn
Level to the mosque, then a steep cemetery path
The courtyard of the Eyüp Sultan mosque
Modest dress; an İstanbulkart for the cable car, which stops in high wind

o-buyukada.name: Büyükada
o-buyukada.teaser: The largest of the Princes' Islands, where the engines are banned and the horses are gone
o-buyukada.story: The Byzantines exiled inconvenient royals to these islands, hence the name. A 1912 census counted about 10,250 Greeks to 670 Turks across them; this was a Greek, Armenian and Jewish summer world, and it is not one now. Private cars are still banned. The horse phaetons went too: glanders broke out among the horses, and a city council decision of 16 January 2020 ended them, with electric carts taking over that summer. Trotsky spent the first four years of his exile here, April 1929 to July 1933, in the Yanaros mansion, now a ruin. The twin domes of the 1911 Splendid Palace mark the waterfront.
o-buyukada.why: Go on a weekday out of high summer, hire a bicycle at the pier and ride away from the quay.
facts: Şehir Hatları from Kabataş, Beşiktaş or Eminönü, about 90 min; from Kadıköy or Bostancı, about 45; boats run round the clock
The climb to Aya Yorgi, its own card

o-st-george.name: Aya Yorgi and the orphanage
o-st-george.teaser: A climb Muslims and Christians make together, past Europe's largest wooden building
o-st-george.story: The path up Yücetepe passes the Prinkipo orphanage, 20,000 square metres of timber designed by Alexandre Vallaury in 1898 as a Wagons-Lits hotel and casino. Abdülhamid II refused the licence; Eleni Zarifi bought it for the Patriarchate, and it took in Greek children from 1903 until the state forced it shut on 21 April 1964. Title came back in 2012, and in 2026 a restoration deal was signed to make it a hotel. At the top, a little over 200 metres up, stands the monastery church of St George, finished in 1909. On 23 April thousands climb for the saint's day, many of them Muslim.
o-st-george.why: Look at the orphanage only from outside, then buy a glass of wine at the monastery café at the top.
facts: Morning; 23 April is the crowded saint's day
The orphanage façade in the pines, exterior only

o-heybeliada.name: Heybeliada
o-heybeliada.teaser: The quiet island next door, with a seminary on the hill that has been shut since 1971
o-heybeliada.story: The Theological School of Halki opened on 1 October 1844 inside the Hagia Triada monastery and trained close to a thousand priests, bishops and patriarchs before Turkey's 1971 ban on private higher education closed it. In 2026 the files moved: the Patriarchate said the renovation would finish in September, and in June Erdoğan ordered talks on reopening, but no opening had been confirmed when we checked. Below, the Naval High School of 1773 keeps the Byzantine Kamariotissa church and the grave of Edward Barton, Elizabeth I's ambassador. The island is 2.35 square kilometres with 4,424 residents in 2022, and small enough to circle by bike in an hour.
o-heybeliada.why: Get off one island early, hire a bike at the jetty and ride the ring road under the pines.

o-anadolu-kavagi.name: Anadolu Kavağı and Yoros Castle
o-anadolu-kavagi.teaser: The whole strait end to end on a commuter boat, and a much-fought-over castle at the top
o-anadolu-kavagi.story: The long Şehir Hatları boat runs from Eminönü up the whole Bosphorus, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı, and holds at Anadolu Kavağı long enough for lunch before turning back. Above the village stands Yoros Castle, Byzantine, Ottoman from 1391, Genoese for some forty years from 1414, which is why everyone still calls it the Genoese castle, then refortified by Mehmed II. It is a steep twenty minutes up from the pier, with the Third Bosphorus Bridge on one side and the open Black Sea on the other. The village below has a mosque of 1593 and a fountain of 1785, and a quay calibrated to the boat.
o-anadolu-kavagi.why: Climb to the castle first, then eat: the view of the Black Sea opening is the point of the day.
facts: Long Bosphorus Tour from Eminönü Boğaz pier; check the day's timetable with Şehir Hatları

o-rumeli-kavagi.name: Rumeli Kavağı
o-rumeli-kavagi.teaser: Get off one stop early, on the European bank: the same fish and a different audience
o-rumeli-kavagi.story: This is the northernmost village on the European side of the strait, and most of its 3,560 residents (2024 count) descend from migrants from the eastern Black Sea, which is what ends up on the plate. The village is known for three things: fish, mussels and figs. A Byzantine fortress stood here until Mehmed II had it pulled down, and excavation has turned up traces of a temple and harbour works beneath the houses. Nearly every boat passenger stays on for the castle across the water, so there are fewer kitchens open and no timetable built around visitors. Balıkçı Kahraman is the table worth the trip.
o-rumeli-kavagi.why: Stop here instead of across the water, and eat whatever came in that morning, cooked plainly.
facts: The last European call on the Long Bosphorus Tour, one stop before Anadolu Kavağı
An afternoon and a long lunch
Rumeli Feneri and Garipçe, a short ride north
Balıkçı Kahraman on İskele Caddesi; mussels on the quay

o-hidiv.name: Hıdiv Kasrı
o-hidiv.teaser: An art nouveau summer palace built in 1907 for the Khedive of Egypt, on a bluff over the strait
o-hidiv.story: Abbas Hilmi Pasha, Khedive of Egypt and nominal Ottoman viceroy of a province richer than most of the empire, built his summer house on this headland above Çubuklu in 1907. It is one of the very few grand houses around Istanbul where you can walk into the rooms rather than photograph a façade, because the building now trades as a restaurant and café inside its own public park, run by the city's Beltur. That means tea, breakfast and grills rather than wine: Time Out lists no alcohol. The climb from the water is a real hill, unpleasant at noon in high summer.
o-hidiv.why: Go for the terrace and the park in the morning, and order tea to walk the rooms.
facts: Çubuklu, Beykoz, on the Asian shore above Kanlıca
Not confirmed for 2026; phone before you go
Morning, before the light goes flat

o-belgrad.name: Belgrad Forest
o-belgrad.teaser: Five and a half thousand hectares of oak, with Istanbul's Ottoman reservoirs hidden in the trees
o-belgrad.story: The name is literal: Süleyman deported Serbs from Belgrade after his 1521 siege and settled them here to keep the city's water running. Two Ottoman systems crossed the forest, the older Kırkçeşme network rebuilt by Sinan and the eighteenth-century Taksim system, whose Mahmud I aqueduct went up at Bahçeköy in 1732. What you walk to are the bents, dammed Ottoman reservoirs, on a 6.5-kilometre marked track from Neşet Suyu among sessile oaks. Sinan's great Mağlova aqueduct, the one in the photographs, is not in this forest at all: it stands in the Alibey valley in Sultangazi.
o-belgrad.why: Start at Bahçeköy early, walk to Büyük Bent and add the Atatürk Arboretum, twenty minutes on.
facts: City bus or car to Bahçeköy, Sarıyer, about an hour from Beyoğlu
Büyük Bent and the 1732 Mahmud I aqueduct
Buy a picnic in Bahçeköy: there are picnic grounds, not restaurants

o-polonezkoy.name: Polonezköy
o-polonezkoy.teaser: A Polish village in the Beykoz forest, founded in 1842 by an exiled prince
o-polonezkoy.story: Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski founded the settlement in 1842 for Poles displaced by the failed November Uprising and named it Adampol. It began with twelve inhabitants and grew with later waves of exiles. Many went home after Poland regained independence in 1918, and those who stayed took Turkish citizenship in 1938. In 2022 the village counted 346 residents, about ninety of them fluent in Polish. What survives is held together by a church, a cemetery and memory: the Zofia Rizi memorial house keeps a village home's photographs, books and original rooms, and 92 graves have been restored.
o-polonezkoy.why: Go midweek for the long forest-edge breakfast; at weekends the single road becomes a queue.
facts: By car or taxi, about 30 km from the historic centre; no useful public transport
The Zofia Rizi memorial house and the church of Our Lady of Częstochowa
Breakfast at the pensions along the village road

o-sile.name: Şile and Ağva
o-sile.teaser: A French-built 1859 lighthouse you can walk into, a crimped cotton cloth and a village between rivers
o-sile.story: The Şile lighthouse was built by French engineers in 1859 for Sultan Abdülmecid and first lit in 1860: a 19-metre octagonal tower with a range of 20 nautical miles, electrified in 1968 and restored by 2022. The town also names Şile bezi, the crimped cotton cloth sold across Istanbul's bazaars. Ağva lies 38 kilometres further east, between the Göksu and the Yeşilçay rivers, which is what its name means, with a long beach and small boats running up the Göksu. The undercurrents on this coast are strong enough that people drown here every summer.
o-sile.why: Swim only between the flags, and stay a night in Ağva on the river rather than drive 97 km twice.
facts: By road; Ağva is about 97 km from the centre and the coast road jams on summer weekends
A full day, better with a night in Ağva
The lighthouse interior, and Şile bezi bought in Şile itself
Riverside pensions on the Göksu in Ağva

c-hagia-sophia.name: Hagia Sophia
c-hagia-sophia.teaser: The first dome fell in 558; the one overhead is the rebuild, and a Norse guard carved his name under it
c-hagia-sophia.story: Justinian's church was inaugurated on 27 December 537, raised in five years and ten months by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. The earthquake of 7 May 558 brought the first dome down; Isidore the Younger rebuilt it higher and steeper by 562, and that is the shell above you. Up in the south gallery, scratched into a marble parapet, are runes found in 1964. Only the ending -ftan survives, read as Halfdan: a Varangian guardsman, bored through a service. A second name, Ári, surfaced in 1975. Cathedral for nine centuries, mosque from 1453, museum from 1935, mosque again since July 2020.
c-hagia-sophia.why: Pay for the upper gallery: it holds the Norse graffiti and the only floor not given over to prayer.
facts: The ground floor is a working prayer hall and closes to visitors around the five daily prayers
EUR 25 for the upper gallery route (seen Aug 2026)
Halfdan's runes, about 23 cm long, on the parapet of the upper south gallery

c-chora.name: Chora — Kariye Mosque
c-chora.teaser: The finest Byzantine mosaic cycle anywhere, and the man who paid for it kneels above the door
c-chora.story: Theodore Metochites, Grand Logothete to Andronikos II, paid for these mosaics and frescoes between about 1315 and 1321, and had himself worked into the panel over the door, handing the church to Christ. He later fell from power and died a monk inside the building he had paid for. It became a mosque in the early sixteenth century, a museum in 1945, and returned to worship, reopening on 6 May 2024 after four years of restoration. Every narthex cycle is on view again. The figural mosaics in the prayer hall are veiled, so the story is told in the two porches.
c-chora.why: Give the two narthexes your full time: that is where the cycle is, and none of it is curtained.
facts: Edirnekapı, Fatih, by the land walls
Daily 09:00-18:00; no visitor entry on Fridays or during the five daily prayers
Metochites in his donor panel above the door into the nave

c-cistern.name: Basilica Cistern
c-cistern.teaser: Two Medusa heads used as column bases, one laid on her side, one upside down
c-cistern.story: Justinian's reservoir was built around 532 under a public basilica, which is where the name comes from. Three hundred and thirty-six columns, most of them taken from older buildings, hold up the roof over water that once fed the Great Palace. In the north-west corner two carved Medusa heads serve as bases, one turned sideways, one inverted, and nothing survives to explain either. It reopened in July 2022 after five years of restoration and seismic work. In June 2026 the state foundations directorate took it over from the city, shut it for four days and reopened it on 6 June; a court challenge to the transfer is still running.
c-cistern.why: Walk straight to the far corner for the Medusas, then come back slowly along the dripping columns.
facts: 1,950 TL by day, 3,000 TL at night (seen Aug 2026); cards and İstanbulkart only, no cash
The two Medusa bases in the north-west corner

c-suleymaniye.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
c-suleymaniye.teaser: Sinan piped the lamp smoke into one room and sent the soot to the palace as ink
c-suleymaniye.story: Begun in 1550 and finished in 1557, it was never only a mosque. Around it Sinan set four madrasas, a medical school, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a caravanserai and a hamam, a whole welfare town on the city's highest hill. Above the entrance he built a chamber that drew the smoke of the oil lamps off the walls, and the collected soot went to the palace calligraphers as ink. Süleyman lies in the garden tomb, Hürrem Sultan in hers of 1558, and Sinan himself in a small tomb at the corner of the wall he built.
c-suleymaniye.why: Finish in the graveyard: the sultan, his wife and his architect lie a few minutes' walk apart.
facts: Süleymaniye, Fatih, above the Golden Horn
Closed to visitors around the five daily prayers
Sinan's own small tomb at the corner of the precinct wall

c-topkapi.name: Topkapı Palace
c-topkapi.teaser: The Quran is read aloud all day in the relic room, and 800 cooks once worked across the courtyard
c-topkapi.story: Mehmed II began it in 1459 and the court ran the empire from here until it moved to Dolmabahçe in 1856. The Chamber of the Sacred Relics has held its collection since 1517, when Selim I took Cairo, and readers still recite the Quran there through opening hours. Down one side of the second courtyard run the kitchens: more than 800 staff cooking for about 4,000 a day, rebuilt by Sinan after the fire of 1574 under ten domes and twenty wide chimneys. That restrained palace style is what Istanbul still means by its own cooking. The rooms now hold 10,700 pieces of Chinese porcelain.
c-topkapi.why: Stand in the relic chamber long enough to hear the reader, then walk the kitchen row.
facts: 2,750 TL for one ticket covering the palace, the Harem and Hagia Irene (seen Aug 2026)
The Spoonmaker's Diamond, 86 carats, and the Topkapı dagger in the Treasury

c-archaeology.name: Istanbul Archaeological Museums
c-archaeology.teaser: A painter dug up the Alexander Sarcophagus, then built a museum around it
c-archaeology.story: In 1887 Osman Hamdi Bey, painter and museum director, excavated the royal necropolis at Sidon and shipped home a sarcophagus of Pentelic marble with its paint still partly legible: Macedonians and Persians fighting in colour. The museum he founded around it opened on 13 June 1891 and holds roughly a million objects, among them two of the three tablets of the Kadesh treaty of about 1259 BC, the oldest known peace treaty; a copy hangs at the United Nations in New York. In September 2026 the complex reopened after a long restoration of the main building, the Ancient Orient museum and the Tiled Kiosk.
c-archaeology.why: Go for the treaty tablets as much as the sarcophagus: a peace deal 3,200 years old, in clay.
facts: Osman Hamdi Bey Yokuşu, Gülhane, Fatih
Reopened in full after restoration, September 2026
Its own ticket, separate from Topkapı
The Alexander Sarcophagus and the Kadesh treaty tablets

c-modern.name: Istanbul Modern
c-modern.teaser: A roof terrace above a sheet of water five centimetres deep, with the old city behind it
c-modern.story: Founded in 2004 as Türkiye's first museum of modern and contemporary art, it began in a 1950s customs warehouse on the Karaköy quay, left in 2018, and came back to the same waterfront on 4 May 2023 in Renzo Piano's first building in the country. Five storeys and 10,500 square metres hold the galleries, a cinema, a library, a café and a restaurant. The aluminium skin is cut to catch the strait's light. On the roof a reflecting pool five centimetres deep faces the historic peninsula and the Galata Tower, so the water on the building and the water below run together.
c-modern.why: Save the last half hour for the roof: the pool and the peninsula line up best from the terrace rail.
facts: Tue-Thu and Sat-Sun 10:00-18:00, Fri to 20:00, closed Mondays (seen Aug 2026)
A weekday morning, before cruise passengers unload onto the same quay

c-pera-museum.name: Pera Museum
c-pera-museum.teaser: An 1893 hotel that now owns the painting that set a Turkish auction record
c-pera-museum.story: The building opened in 1893 as the Bristol, one of the Pera hotels that took Orient Express traffic alongside the Pera Palace and the Tokatlıyan. Its facade was kept and everything behind it rebuilt as galleries, and the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation opened the museum on 8 June 2005. The anchor is Osman Hamdi Bey's The Tortoise Trainer of 1906: an old man in a dervish robe, a flute on his back, trying to teach five tortoises. The foundation bought it at auction in December 2004 for what was then a record for a Turkish work.
c-pera-museum.why: Come on a Friday evening, when entry is free and the tortoises keep their late hours.
facts: Tue-Sat 10:00-19:00, Fri to 22:00, Sun 12:00-18:00, closed Mondays (seen Aug 2026)
300 TL (seen Aug 2026); free Fridays 18:00-22:00, free for students on Wednesdays
The Tortoise Trainer, Osman Hamdi Bey, 1906

c-cicek.name: Çiçek Pasajı
c-cicek.teaser: An arcade built on the ashes of the empire's opera house, named for Russian flower sellers
c-cicek.story: The Naum Theatre stood here, the Ottoman capital's chief opera house, staging Verdi with Sultans Abdülaziz and Abdülhamid II in the audience, until the Pera fire of 1870. The Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos bought the ruin and had Kleanthis Zannos build the Cité de Péra on it in 1876: twenty-four shops below, eighteen apartments above. Destitute Russian noblewomen who arrived after 1917 sold flowers in the corridor, and the name stuck. Later the shops became rough meyhanes, told in the food-history fold. The building failed in 1978 and was rebuilt by 1988, with more work in 2005 and 2022. The clientele never came back.
c-cicek.why: Walk the arcade for the ironwork and the history, then eat somewhere else.
facts: A public arcade off the avenue
The 1876 facade on İstiklal, the Cité de Péra name above the door

c-zeki-muren.name: Zeki Müren
c-zeki-muren.teaser: Turkey's most loved voice belonged to its most flamboyant man, and a conservative public never minded
c-zeki-muren.story: Born in Bursa in 1931 and schooled in Istanbul, he entered the State Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 and made his first live broadcast on Istanbul Radio on 1 January 1951. For eleven years he then held the stage at the Maksim gazino in Taksim, the orchestra-backed big room that grew out of the meyhane's fasıl nights. He wore a sequinned jacket in 1958 and a miniskirt in 1970, and the country called him Sanat Güneşi, the Sun of Art. He collapsed and died at a TRT ceremony on 24 September 1996, leaving everything to two charitable foundations.
c-zeki-muren.why: Hear him before you judge him: one fasıl record explains the affection better than any photograph.
facts: Taksim, where the Maksim gazino stood until it closed in 2005; the site is now a hotel

c-black-russian.name: The Black Russian
c-black-russian.teaser: The man who brought jazz to Istanbul was born in Mississippi to parents freed from slavery
c-black-russian.story: Frederick Bruce Thomas was born in Coahoma County, Mississippi, in November 1872, to parents who had been enslaved. He reached Moscow by way of London and ran theatres and restaurants there for nineteen years, until the revolution sent him south to Constantinople. He opened Stella in Şişli, then Maxim in Taksim in 1921, and through him the city heard the foxtrot, the Charleston and live jazz. Refused a United States passport and buried in debt, he died in a debtors' prison in June 1928. The Maxim name outlived him on Taksim for almost eighty years.
c-black-russian.why: Read Alexandrov's biography before a night out in Beyoğlu: the jazz you hear there starts with him.
facts: Şişli and Taksim, the two districts where he opened his clubs
The Istanbul chapter rests largely on one biographer, Vladimir Alexandrov

c-yenikapi.name: Yenikapı — the dig that held up the railway
c-yenikapi.teaser: Digging for the rail tunnel turned up 37 ships and footprints 8,500 years old
c-yenikapi.story: Salvage excavation at Yenikapı ran from 2004 to 2013 and held the Marmaray rail project up for years. It exposed the Theodosian Harbour and thirty-seven shipwrecks of the fifth to eleventh centuries, the largest group of medieval ships ever found on one site. Below the harbour floor lay something far older: house foundations, burials and human footprints from roughly 8,500 years ago, when the Sea of Marmara was still a lake. Sixty thousand objects came out in all. The site itself is now a transport interchange, and thousands of commuters change trains each day above a vanished port.
c-yenikapi.why: Change trains at Yenikapı once knowing what is under the platform; the city rarely shows its depth so plainly.
facts: The finds are held by the Istanbul Archaeological Museums, which reopened after restoration in September 2026

c-tunel.name: Tünel
c-tunel.teaser: Twelve years after London, the second underground railway on earth, all 573 metres of it
c-tunel.story: The French engineer Eugène-Henri Gavand built it to solve exactly one problem: the climb from the port at Galata to the merchant quarter at Pera. It opened on 17 January 1875, which makes it the second-oldest underground urban railway in the world, after London's of 1863. It runs 573 metres and rises about sixty. Steam drove it until the renovation that closed the line in 1968; electrified, it reopened in 1971 and still does the only job it was ever built for, carrying people up the hill in well under two minutes.
c-tunel.why: Ride it uphill rather than walking: two minutes on the world's second underground saves the steepest climb in Beyoğlu.
facts: Karaköy station to Tünel Meydanı, Beyoğlu
A ride of well under two minutes
The upper exit, which leads straight onto İstiklal and the top of Galip Dede Caddesi

l-hippodrome.name: Sultanahmet Meydanı — the Hippodrome
l-hippodrome.teaser: You are standing on the racetrack, about 450 metres of it, under two metres of fill
l-hippodrome.story: Septimius Severus laid a hippodrome here around AD 203, and Constantine rebuilt it in 324-330 for some 100,000 spectators. The long oval of the square is the track; its monuments mark the spina the chariots turned around, in pits because the ground has risen about two metres. The granite obelisk was cut for Thutmose III around 1450 BC and raised again here by Theodosius I in 390, on a base showing him watching the races. Beside it stand the Serpent Column, cast from Persian weapons after Plataea in 479 BC, and the Walled Obelisk, stripped of its bronze in 1204. The Nika riots started here.
l-hippodrome.why: Read the obelisk's base: an emperor in his box, carved in Constantinople, watching the races you are standing on.
facts: 07:00 before the coaches, or after dark when it is floodlit and the touts have gone
The Serpent Column from Delphi, the oldest Greek object in the city

l-beyazit.name: Beyazıt Meydanı
l-beyazit.teaser: The university's square, laid over the biggest forum of Roman Constantinople
l-beyazit.story: Under the paving lies the Forum of Theodosius, the Forum Tauri. Around it stands a full Ottoman-to-Republic set: the Beyazıt II Mosque on one side, the Neo-Renaissance gate of Istanbul University by the French architect Bourgeois on the other, the Beyazıt Tower behind, and the State Library of 1884 between them, whose renovation found a Byzantine church under the floor. The square was rebuilt and reopened on 6 October 2022, and it is now the calmest large open space in the old city: students on the steps, seed sellers and their clouds of pigeons, old men on benches under the planes.
l-beyazit.why: Sit with a tea under the plane trees on the mosque side, then drop down the lane to the book market.
facts: Open ground, at any hour; on demonstration days expect police barriers
Late afternoon, when the light runs low across the mosque courtyard
The university gate and the tower behind it

l-ortakoy.name: Ortaköy Meydanı
l-ortakoy.teaser: The one square in the city that sits on the Bosphorus, with a Balyan mosque on the quay
l-ortakoy.story: The Büyük Mecidiye Camii, which everyone calls the Ortaköy Mosque, was built in 1854-56 for Sultan Abdülmecid I by Garabet and Nigoğayos Balyan, the Armenian father and son who built Dolmabahçe. It stands not by the water but on it, Baroque stone carving rising straight out of the strait, and it came back from a three-year restoration on 6 June 2014. Behind it the lanes run kumpir stalls, the loaded baked potato that is Ortaköy's street dish, and café tables to the edge. From the quay rail the 1850s mosque and the first Bosphorus bridge share one frame while ferries slide between them.
l-ortakoy.why: Take the photograph from the quay rail on a weekday morning, when the fishermen are the only crowd.
facts: Open ground at any hour; the mosque outside prayer times
Weekday morning; sunset is the picture, but weekend afternoons are shoulder to shoulder
The mosque against the 15 Temmuz Şehitler Köprüsü from the rail

l-gulhane.name: Gülhane Parkı
l-gulhane.teaser: The outer garden of Topkapı Palace, and the city's oldest public park, no ticket needed
l-gulhane.story: This was the wooded outer garden of Topkapı, opened to the public by the municipality in 1912: just under ten hectares falling from the palace walls toward Sarayburnu, where the Bosphorus meets the Marmara. The Tanzimat edict, the decree that began the empire's modernisation, was read here on 3 November 1839. The old zoo and funfair are gone. What is left is lawns, very old planes with grey herons in them, and the Goths Column, a Roman victory monument, near the lower end. The Alay Köşkü sits on the outer wall and the Islamic science museum fills the old stables.
l-gulhane.why: Walk downhill under the planes to the Goths Column: the palace's ground, free, two minutes from the tram.
facts: Gated city park; go in daylight, and expect it shut on severe-storm alerts
The Goths Column at the lower end of the park

l-emirgan.name: Emirgan Korusu
l-emirgan.teaser: A khedive's exile estate above the Bosphorus, and every April the densest flowerbed in Turkey
l-emirgan.story: Forty-seven hectares of grove above the Emirgan shore were the estate of Khedive İsmail Paşa of Egypt, who lived out his exile here; the city took it over in the 1940s and İBB runs it now. His three nineteenth-century pavilions survive, restored in 1979-83: the yellow Sarı Köşk, the white Beyaz Köşk and the pink Pembe Köşk, all now municipal cafés. Since 2005 the April tulip festival has used Emirgan as its main stage, millions of bulbs in set-piece beds, and the shore road jams. In any other month you get steep paths, ponds, huge pines and the strait flashing between trunks.
l-emirgan.why: Come outside April and look at the Sarı Köşk across the pond in silence.
facts: Emirgan, Sarıyer, on the European shore
Pavilion café hours unverified; the grove is the point
Any month but April; in tulip season come by bus or ferry and walk up
The Sakıp Sabancı Museum at the foot of the hill, told in the craft fold

l-fethi-pasa.name: Fethi Paşa Korusu
l-fethi-pasa.teaser: A vizier's grove on the Asian shore, with the first bridge filling the whole view
l-fethi-pasa.story: Some thirteen hectares of wooded hillside drop to the Bosphorus just north of Üsküdar, named for Fethi Ahmed Paşa, the Ottoman vizier whose estate this was. After decades of neglect it was renewed and opened fully to the public, and it is steeper and quieter than the European shore's parks. The terraces point straight at the water: Ortaköy and the European towers opposite, the first Bosphorus bridge overhead, close enough to read the traffic. A municipal facility, the Fethipaşa Sosyal Tesisi, serves tea and breakfast in the grove, and this is where Üsküdar families come for Sunday breakfast.
l-fethi-pasa.why: Have breakfast on the upper terrace: the bridge panorama, and not one tour group in sight.
facts: Paşalimanı, Üsküdar, between Kuzguncuk and Sultantepe
Facility hours unverified; the terraces are free and always there
Breakfast time, walking in from Kuzguncuk
The bridge from the upper terrace; wear flat shoes for the steep paths

l-valide-han.name: Büyük Valide Han
l-valide-han.teaser: The largest caravanserai in the city still works, and no, you cannot go on the roof
l-valide-han.story: Kösem Sultan, mother of two sultans and for a time the most powerful woman in Ottoman history, built it around 1651 to fund her Çinili complex: 210 rooms around three courtyards. It was the base of the Iranian merchant colony, whose small Shia mescit still stands in the courtyard; Muharram ceremonies were held here until 1927. The third courtyard is largely ruinous, with the Byzantine Tower of Eirene at its corner, yet foundry and mould-making workshops still trade in the galleries. The famous roof was closed by the culture ministry in 2016 after visitors damaged the domes, and a fire broke out on it in June 2026.
l-valide-han.why: Come for the working courtyards, not the roof: a seventeenth-century han still doing its first job.
facts: Mercan, Fatih, uphill from the Grand Bazaar

l-rustem-pasa.name: Rüstem Paşa Camii
l-rustem-pasa.teaser: Sinan's tile box, up a stair above the market whose rents pay for it
l-rustem-pasa.story: The mosque sits on a raised terrace above a block of vaulted shops in Tahtakale, reached by a stair off the market street that is easy to walk past. The shops are the point: their rents endowed the mosque, trade below and prayer above. Sinan finished it around 1563 for Rüstem Paşa, Süleyman's grand vizier and husband of Mihrimah Sultan. Inside, some 2,300 İznik tiles in about eighty patterns cover the walls, including the tomato red of Armenian bole, a colour the İznik kilns mastered for a few decades in the sixteenth century and then lost. It reopened for worship in 2021.
l-rustem-pasa.why: Give your eyes ten minutes, then find the tomato red near the qibla wall.
facts: Tahtakale, Eminönü, beside the Spice Bazaar
Working mosque; closed to visits during the five daily prayers

l-kucuk-ayasofya.name: Küçük Ayasofya Camii
l-kucuk-ayasofya.teaser: Justinian's other great church: older ground, no queue, no ticket
l-kucuk-ayasofya.story: Ten minutes downhill from the Sultanahmet queues stands the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, begun by Justinian early in his reign. Scholars date it between 527 and 536, some arguing for the mid-520s, so it may be older than the great Hagia Sophia. Around the interior runs the original Greek frieze naming Justinian and the empress Theodora, and mentioning Saint Sergius while leaving Saint Bacchus out. Hüseyin Ağa, the palace's chief eunuch, made it a mosque between 1506 and 1513. Restored through 2006, it is now a quiet neighbourhood mosque: an octagon under a dome, carved marble, carpet underfoot.
l-kucuk-ayasofya.why: Stand alone in a sixth-century imperial building while the crowds wait up the hill.
facts: Küçük Ayasofya, Fatih, below the Hippodrome
Working mosque; visit outside prayer times, shoes off, shoulders covered
The marble frieze that still names Justinian and Theodora

x-ebristan.name: Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil
x-ebristan.teaser: A living marbling master, his own pattern named gunpowder, and a studio that still teaches
x-ebristan.story: Ebru is pigment ground from earth and mineral, cut with ox gall so it floats, dropped onto water thickened with tragacanth, combed into tulips, stones and waves, then lifted off in one sheet. It was made for bookbinders as endpapers and as a ground for documents no one could forge twice; UNESCO inscribed it in 2014. Hikmet Barutçugil, born in Malatya in 1952, trained as a textile designer and turned to marbling in 1977. He opened Ebristan in Salacak in 1996 and still teaches there, pupil by pupil. One pattern carries his name: barut ebrusu, gunpowder marbling.
x-ebristan.why: This is the one because the craft is living, the master is named, and you learn at his own tray.
facts: Ebru, Turkish marbling, inscribed by UNESCO in 2014 and still handed from master to pupil
Hikmet Barutçugil, marbling since 1977, his studio since 1996

By arrangement only: no public course calendar or online booking found (Oct 2026); contact Ebristan directly

x-caferaga.name: Caferağa Medresesi
x-caferaga.teaser: Sinan's medrese behind Hagia Sophia, still teaching the crafts in its old student cells
x-caferaga.story: Mimar Sinan built this medrese for Cafer Ağa in 1559, in the reign of Süleyman, immediately behind Hagia Sophia. Since 1989 the Türk Kültürüne Hizmet Vakfı has run it as a working crafts school, and the old student cells around the courtyard now hold ebru, hüsn-i hat, tezhip gilding, çini, miniature, stained glass, jewellery, felt and weaving. Full courses run over months, and shorter sessions exist for visitors. What it lacks is a face: no teacher is named publicly, so you cannot know whose hand you are learning from until you are in the room.
x-caferaga.why: The courtyard alone is worth five minutes off the Sultanahmet crowds, class or no class.
facts: A named master: the teachers are not listed publicly
Ebru, calligraphy, gilding, tile, miniature and more, taught in the cells
Full courses run over months; shorter visitor sessions exist

x-cini.name: Çini — the İznik blue
x-cini.teaser: A Turkish word that means Chinese, and it is being honest
x-cini.story: Çini is Çin, China, with an ending: Ottoman potters were chasing the prestige of imported Chinese blue-and-white, and the language kept the receipt. The İznik body is the trick, up to eighty-five per cent quartz, which is why the glaze looks lit from behind. Production stopped in the seventeenth century and the recipe died with it. The İznik Foundation, set up in 1993 by the economist Işıl Akbaygil, reverse-engineered the quartz body and was firing again from 1995. UNESCO listed the craft in 2016. The kilns are in İznik, in Bursa province, not here.
x-cini.why: See the old İznik red at Rüstem Paşa before you buy any tile, so you know what the real thing does to light.
facts: A named Istanbul studio where a visitor can learn it; the craft is fired in İznik
Look, then buy: the tiles are sold in Istanbul, made in İznik
Caferağa Medresesi lists çini among its courses; ask at the gate

x-hat.name: Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy
x-hat.teaser: Writing measured in dots, where the shape of the letter is the whole point
x-hat.story: Ottoman calligraphy is written to proportion: every letter is measured in rhombic dots laid down by the same reed pen, so a hand is judged on its geometry before its words. The kit never changes: reed pen, trimming slab, soot ink, paper sized and burnished until ink cannot bleed. Istanbul set the proportions the rest of the Islamic world copied, teacher to pupil, by licence; UNESCO inscribed it in 2021. To see it, go to the Atlı Köşk at Emirgan, a 1927 villa by Edouard De Nari, where Sakıp Sabancı's five centuries of Qur'ans, panels and imperial documents have been a museum since 2002.
x-hat.why: Look for the first piece he bought, a panel by Sultan Mahmud II: the collection grew from it.
facts: A class to join: this is a craft to look at here, not to try
See it at the Sakıp Sabancı Museum: Qur'ans, hilyes, albums and calligraphic panels

x-carpets.name: Carpets and "antiques" — the honest note
x-carpets.teaser: If it is genuinely antique, you are not allowed to take it home
x-carpets.story: Turkish law protects cultural property, and genuinely old carpets, tiles, coins and icons cannot legally leave the country. Dealers who sell older pieces are expected to hand over museum certification that an item is not an antiquity, which tells you exactly what the three-hundred-year-old rug on the wall is. A reputable seller produces that paperwork without being asked. Then turn the rug over: a hand-knotted back is slightly irregular, a machine-made one suspiciously perfect. The rule holds anywhere in Turkey, not only inside the bazaar.
x-carpets.why: Ask for the museum paper before you ask the price; a dealer who hesitates has answered you.
facts: Turn any rug over in any shop: irregular knots on the back mean hand-made

a-grand-bazaar.name: Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar
a-grand-bazaar.teaser: Sixty-one streets named for guilds that mostly no longer trade on them, and gold sold at the day's rate
a-grand-bazaar.story: Mehmed II began it within three years of the conquest; the stone bedesten for cloth and gems was finished by 1461, and it grew to sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops over 30,700 square metres. Every lane was a guild, and the names record trades that have since left. Kalpakçılar Caddesi, the main artery, is Hatmakers' Street and has not sold a fur hat in living memory: it is gold end to end. Turkish households save in gold because the lira keeps falling, so these jewellers serve locals, and the price is arithmetic: the day's gram rate plus workmanship.
a-grand-bazaar.why: Ask for the gram rate and the labour charge separately, and the haggle turns into a talk about who made the piece.
facts: Monday to Saturday; closed Sundays and religious holidays
Kalpakçılar Caddesi, Beyazıt gate to Nuruosmaniye gate, for the gold

a-zincirli.name: Zincirli Han
a-zincirli.teaser: The courtyard where the hammering is real and nobody chases you
a-zincirli.story: Built in 1708 on the caravanserai plan, shops below and workshops and lodgings above, Zincirli was the bazaar's han for goldsmiths and jewellers, with carpet and antique dealers alongside. It is the quietest courtyard in the bazaar and still the most working one. Behind the shopfronts metal is melted and copper is hammered by ateliers that have run for generations. The master-and-apprentice chain has thinned badly, but it has not broken. Stand still in the middle for a few minutes and the place tells you more than any sales pitch.
a-zincirli.why: Go on a weekday morning, stand still in the courtyard and listen to the hammers.
facts: The workshops behind the shopfronts, where metal is melted and hammered

a-sahaflar.name: Sahaflar Çarşısı
a-sahaflar.teaser: A book market on Byzantine ground, now mostly selling exam crammers
a-sahaflar.story: The booksellers' courtyard between the Grand Bazaar and the Beyazıt Mosque stands on the Chartoprateia, the Byzantine paper and book market, so the trade has not moved in a thousand years. Sahaf is Arabic for a dealer in written sheets. Ottoman booksellers left the bazaar for this yard in the eighteenth century; fire took it in the 1950s and it was rebuilt. The honest picture now: computers and then the internet hollowed out the antiquarian trade, and much of the stock is exam crammers. The odd old print still waits on a back shelf for anyone patient enough to ask.
a-sahaflar.why: Walk through on your way from the bazaar to Beyazıt: a thousand years of one trade on one spot.
facts: The few antiquarian dealers among the exam-book stalls

a-galip-dede.name: Galip Dede Caddesi — the music street
a-galip-dede.teaser: The whole instrument trade on one downhill street, the good hung beside the useless
a-galip-dede.story: The street falls from Tünel to the Galata Tower and has been the musicians' bazaar for decades: darbuka, davul and frame drums, bağlama and saz, ney and zurna, string sellers and repair benches behind the counters. The names on the shop signs come from four directions. Saz is Persian for instrument. Bağlama comes from bağlamak, to tie, after the gut frets tied round the neck. Kanun is Greek kanōn, the rule that sets the pitch. Ud is Arabic al-ʿūd, the wood, the root of our lute. A large share of the bağlamas in the windows are decorative and close to unplayable.
a-galip-dede.why: Ask to hear an instrument played before you buy; if nobody in the shop can play it, that is your answer.
facts: The repair benches behind the counters, and a bağlama someone will play for you

a-manol.name: Manol, and who actually built the oud
a-manol.teaser: The Turkish oud has an inventor, and his name was Manol
a-manol.story: The Metropolitan Museum in New York, which owns one of his instruments, records Emmanuel Venios, known as Manol, as Greek, born on Folegandros about 1838 and dead in Istanbul in 1915 or 1916. He had a workshop on İstiklal by about 1870, and he is credited with the smaller, higher-tuned instrument the world now calls the Turkish oud; his are still held to be the finest ever built. The other great maker of the tradition, Onnik Karibyan, working a generation later, was Armenian. The instrument at the centre of Turkish classical music was shaped by communities this city lost.
a-manol.why: Ask an oud maker on Galip Dede whose pattern his instruments follow; Manol's name usually comes up.
facts: The living oud trade on Galip Dede Caddesi, downhill from Tünel
His death year: the Met gives 1915 or 1916

a-lale-plak.name: Lale Plak
a-lale-plak.teaser: Half a century at the top of the music street, run by one ear
a-lale-plak.story: At the Tünel end of the music street, Lale Plak is among the oldest record shops in the city, trading for well over fifty years, though the sources disagree on the exact founding year. Hakan Atala's stock runs from Western classical and jazz, signed pressings among them, to the 1970s Turkish canon: Barış Manço, Ajda Pekkan, the Anadolu rock years. It is a narrow shop to be served in rather than browsed. Say what you are after, a singer, a decade or a mood, and let him pull it from the shelves behind the counter.
a-lale-plak.why: Tell Hakan Atala what you like and let him choose; that is how the shop is meant to work.
facts: Anadolu rock and 1970s Turkish pressings, and signed classical and jazz records
The founding year; all agree on more than fifty years

h-sequence.name: The sequence, start to finish
h-sequence.teaser: Cold hall, hot marble, scrub, foam, rinse: ninety minutes to two hours, and nothing planned after
h-sequence.story: In the camekân, the cold domed hall, you take a numbered key and a cabin, strip and wrap. Then the hararet: you lie on the göbek taşı, the marble platform heated from below, until you sweat properly, because the scrub fails on cold skin. Only then does the attendant come with the kese, a coarse mitt that lifts dead skin in grey rolls. Foam follows, poured from a cloth bag, then hair, then rinsing with a bowl from the kurna, the basin you never climb into. You finish wrapped in dry cotton with tea. There is no sauna and no pool: Ottoman bathing never had either.
h-sequence.why: Know the order before you undress: at the busy restored houses nobody walks you through it unless you ask.

h-gender.name: Gendered hours — the way this trip actually fails
h-gender.teaser: Nine houses, four systems, two that never say which half runs when. Get it wrong and the door is locked
h-gender.story: Istanbul has no single rule. Some baths are çifte, twin buildings with a men's half and a women's half behind separate street doors. Some are one bath sliced by the clock, with a dead changeover between. Two are mixed and take any party of men and women together. Two describe separate sections yet publish one undifferentiated hours line. Two traps bite hardest: the last reservation is often hours before closing, and third-party listings lag behind the houses' own pages. A woman reaching Kılıç Ali Paşa at five in the afternoon does not get in; a man arriving there at eleven in the morning is turned away too.
h-gender.why: Phone the house the morning you go: the closing time on the door is not the time you can still walk in.

h-money.name: The money, the extras, and who is refused
h-money.teaser: The massage is never in the bath price, cash beats card, and some houses turn guests away at the door
h-money.story: The bath price has never included an oil massage. Kılıç Ali Paşa and Galatasaray say so in writing: a massage means a separate room, therapist, booking and bill, and at Kılıç Ali Paşa it costs more than the ritual itself. Expect it offered warmly while you are wet, wrapped and in no position to haggle. Decide before you go in, ask for the all-in total rather than the door price, and separate your tip notes before you undress. The houses also take medicine seriously: this is a room near 40°C and 70% humidity with a stranger pressing on you for half an hour, and some will refuse you.
h-money.why: Settle the total and the tip at the desk, dry and dressed; done later, in a wrap, it always costs more.

h-kilic-ali.name: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı
h-kilic-ali.teaser: Sinan's bath for the crews of the Ottoman fleet: one dome, no second wing, and the clock decides who enters
h-kilic-ali.story: Mimar Sinan built this bath in the late 1570s inside admiral Kılıç Ali Pasha's mosque complex for the levends, the crews of the Ottoman fleet, when Tophane was the working harbour. The patron was born Giovanni Dionigi Galeni in Calabria, set to the oars as a galley slave, converted and rose to command the navy; Cervantes calls him Uchali. The hot room is one great volume under a dome fourteen metres wide and seventeen high, the house says the city's second-largest. Seven years of restoration ended in 2012, and Europa Nostra honoured it in 2017. There is no second wing: one bath, alternating by the clock.
h-kilic-ali.why: The best first hammam: one great dome and a ritual the house documents step by illustrated step.

h-zeyrek.name: Zeyrek Çinili Hamam
h-zeyrek.teaser: The grand admiral's bath, back in service after thirteen years of restoration, with a museum under the marble
h-zeyrek.story: Barbaros Hayreddin Paşa, grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet, commissioned it, and the house credits Mimar Sinan, building over a Byzantine cistern under Süleyman the Magnificent. The İznik tiles that named it left long ago for European collections. After a thirteen-year restoration under The Marmara Group it reopened in September 2023, and it is a museum as well as a bath: in the cistern below the women's cold room, plaster carries incised graffiti of galleys whose makers and date nobody knows. Every treatment ends back in the cold room with a rose-geranium towel for the face, Turkish tea and something sweet and savoury.
h-zeyrek.why: Go for the cistern graffiti and the polished dome; take The DIY if you would rather not be handled.

h-cagaloglu.name: Cağaloğlu Hamamı
h-cagaloglu.teaser: The last great bath the empire built in the city, and it was built to pay for a library
h-cagaloglu.story: Built in 1741 under Mahmud I, begun by the architect Süleyman Ağa and finished by Abdullah Ağa, it was endowed as a çifte bath to fund the sultan's library inside Hagia Sophia: the bath paid for the books. The house calls it the last of its kind built in Istanbul. Men climb ten steps between two marble columns with stalactite capitals, under an inscription of seven lines and twenty-eight verses; the steps exist because the street rose over three centuries. Inside the men's camekân a high dome with a lantern at its crown stands over a pool and a water jet. Women enter from another street entirely.
h-cagaloglu.why: Choose it for the 1741 architecture and lunch in the same building; the room itself is almost all visitors.

h-suleymaniye.name: Süleymaniye Hamamı
h-suleymaniye.teaser: Oak-fired around the clock, and the bath where a mixed party of men and women goes in through one door
h-suleymaniye.story: The house trades on 'Since 1550' and credits Mimar Sinan, though its own FAQ arithmetic lands nearer 1554. Two things set it apart. The first is the furnace: oak fires burn under the floor day and night, holding the hot room at 38 to 40°C. The second is the format. In its main session it takes mixed parties, any party of men and women together, family included, in one shared communal room, and it will not separate them: scrub and soap massage are taken side by side beside the kurna. The house page read in August said every tellak is male, for every guest, women included.
h-suleymaniye.why: The one bath where a mixed party bathes together; read the booking rules before you commit a day off.

r-tiras.name: Tıraş — the full berber
r-tiras.teaser: Cut, cut-throat shave, ear-singe, cologne: a licensed trade, with a printed tariff you may ask to see
r-tiras.story: The berber is a licensed trade with its own chamber, and licensed shops display a tarife, so asking to see the price list is normal here. The full saç sakal runs haircut, hot towel, brush lather, then the ustura, the open razor, with the grain and against it. A flame flicks over the ears to take the fine hair; it lasts two seconds and does not hurt. Alum on the nicks, a second towel, then lemon cologne poured into your cupped hands. Behind Hagia Sophia, Rimedzo has kept the same doorway since 1986 and tells you to read its list before you sit.
r-tiras.why: Forty-five minutes in the chair is the most Istanbul thing a man can do for the price of lunch.

r-sema.name: Sema — ceremony or show
r-sema.teaser: The tall felt hat and the white skirt appear at every tier. The costume never tells you what you bought
r-sema.story: UNESCO proclaimed the Mevlevi Sema a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. What is protected is the ayin, a fixed four-part musical form for voice, ney, kudüm drum and cymbals, and the turn itself: left foot planted, right palm up to receive, left palm down to give. The Republic closed every tekke in 1925, and what survived of the order survived as culture on a stage, so the blur between rite and show is the price of its survival. The useful test is the room: a theatre with a foyer, or a hall where people also pray.
r-sema.why: Decide which you want, prayer or performance, and buy that honestly; both are worth an evening.
facts: A foundation's own ayin with no ticket desk; a ticketed sema in a real semahane such as Galata; a purpose-built show in a culture centre, such as Hodjapasha in Sirkeci (unconfirmed as running)
Whirling sold with dinner and belly dancing is the bottom tier, whatever the poster says
No applause and no flash, do not leave while they turn; long sleeves and trousers, women cover the head at a foundation, shoes off on a prayer floor
Deliberately not quoted: check the seller's own page on the day
The Saturday evening at the Silivrikapı foundation, or the Galata lodge's semahane by daylight
Resale platforms quote prices nobody can verify, and the one sema price on the official museum listing is years out of date

r-emav.name: Silivrikapı Mevlana Kültür Merkezi (EMAV)
r-emav.teaser: A foundation's own sema twice a week, the discourse subtitled in English, no ticket desk: phone for the door
r-emav.story: Evrensel Mevlana Aşıkları Vakfı runs its own weekly evenings at the Silivrikapı Mevlana Cultural Center, the house associated with Hasan Dede, who spent his life teaching there. For a non-Turkish speaker the rare thing is that the opening discourse is a recorded video with English subtitles, so you follow the evening rather than merely watch it. Partway through comes the ikram, food and drink offered to everyone sitting on the floor: the sign that you are a guest at somebody's evening, not an audience. Arrive for the start; slipping in at the end to catch the turning is what everyone notices.
r-emav.why: The closest a visitor gets to the rite itself, with subtitles, and it asks nothing at the door.
facts: Thursday 19:30–22:30, sema from 21:40; Saturday 19:00–20:30, sema from 19:50 (seen Aug 2026); moves for religious dates
The foundation names the Silivrikapı hall but prints no street address, only its Şehremini office: phone before you set out
No admission published; carry cash for a donation
Long sleeves and trousers, women cover the head, shoes off; you sit on the floor

r-galata-mevlevi.name: Galata Mevlevihanesi
r-galata-mevlevi.teaser: A 1491 lodge with a genuine semahane: visit it as a museum, and treat the ceremony as a maybe
r-galata-mevlevi.story: Founded in 1491 and known in Ottoman times as the Kulekapısı lodge, this is the one place a visitor can stand inside a real semahane on an ordinary weekday. It closed with every tekke in 1925, reopened as a museum in 1975 and was reorganised as the Mevlevi lodge museum in 2011. The hall is the reason: a wooden floor, mihrab and minber at the far end, the gallery where the musicians sat. Side rooms hold marbling, calligraphy and hilye sheets, and the courtyard holds the tomb of the poet Şeyh Galib, once sheikh here. It crowns Galip Dede Caddesi, the instrument-makers' street.
r-galata-mevlevi.why: Walk up from Karaköy past the instrument shops and have the semahane almost to yourself.
facts: Şahkulu Mah., Galip Dede Cad. No:15, Beyoğlu; +90 212 245 41 41
Tue–Sun, closed Mondays; 09:00–18:30 per the museum listing, 09:00–16:30 per OpenStreetMap, box office shuts an hour before (seen Aug 2026)
Listed Sunday 18:00, one hour, 150 unnumbered seats, but run by an outside ensemble on an intermittent calendar: phone before you plan an evening
Shoes off on the semahane floor; at a ceremony, silence, no flash, no applause
The gallery: look down into the semahane from where the musicians sat

r-cay.name: Çay bahçesi — the price of a chair
r-cay.teaser: One glass of tea buys the table for as long as you want it. That is the whole contract, and it holds
r-cay.story: Law 407 of 1924 put tea growing on a legal footing at Rize on the wet Black Sea coast, to bring work to the east after the First World War; the first large harvest came in 1938, the first factory in 1947. Within a generation the glass ran the whole day. In a çay bahçesi one glass buys the table for as long as you like. It comes thin-waisted on a saucer with two sugar cubes, poured from a stacked double pot, brew above and hot water below, mixed to your order. Grandparents hold tables for four hours over backgammon. Nobody is moved on.
r-cay.why: A few small glasses rent you a view for the whole afternoon.
facts: 'Bir çay' for one, 'iki çay' for a pair; açık for pale, koyu for dark; refills one glass at a time
Sit anywhere free, a waiter with a tray finds you; pay at the end, often in cash
Tea, Turkish coffee and little else, no music, and your own food welcome
No milk; round up rather than tip; share the table when asked, not the conversation; refusing an offered glass is close to rude
Deliberately not quoted: a municipal garden costs a fraction of a waterfront one pouring the same glass
Çınaraltı at Çengelköy, Pierre Loti above Eyüp, Moda Aile, Çadır Köşkü in Yıldız: each has its own card

r-nargile.name: Nargile — the medrese and the Tophane strip
r-nargile.teaser: If the pipe arrives in under ten minutes it was not built for you. The whole point is the two hours
r-nargile.story: Nargile reached Ottoman Istanbul in the seventeenth century, and Murad IV banned it alongside coffee and tobacco on the reasoning that men who sit together talk. Most of what is smoked now is mu'assel, tobacco cut with molasses and fruit; the older tömbeki, plain soaked leaf under raw coal, is harsher and slower, and still served if you ask for it by name. In the medrese Çorlulu Ali Paşa built in 1708 on the old Divanyolu, two courtyards of carpet dealers hold one of the city's long-standing nargile gardens: low stools, cushions, and a boy with tongs working the coals.
r-nargile.why: The cheapest way in the city to hold a table for a whole evening, if you accept what you are smoking.
facts: Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi, Yeniçeriler Cad., Beyazıt, between the Grand Bazaar and Çemberlitaş; or the Tophane strip below İstiklal, where shop names turn over fast
'Nargile' and a flavour, or simply 'elma', apple; 'köz alabilir miyim?' for fresh coals
Not quoted: ask before the pipe is packed; the medrese is visitor-priced, Tophane runs at neighbourhood rates
A coal boy on the floor with tongs and a brazier, not a waiter with a lighter
Pass the hose by the stem; never light a cigarette from the coal; expect no alcohol
This is tobacco smoked for an hour or two; the water does not make it mild

r-kahve.name: Türk kahvesi — the cup, and the cup turned over
r-kahve.teaser: One small cup, twenty minutes, a foam you judge it by, and the grounds left for a stranger to read
r-kahve.story: Hakem of Aleppo and Şems of Damascus opened Istanbul's first coffeehouse in Tahtakale in 1554, and UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture in 2013 for the ritual rather than the bean: water first, a sweet alongside, grounds left in the cup for the fal. The cup is judged on the köpük, the fine foam, which comes from bringing the cezve up slowly and lifting it off as it rises, never letting it boil. Fazıl Bey's market-side Kadıköy counter does it properly at an everyday price. Turn the cup onto its saucer, let it cool, and in Kadıköy a falcı will read the grounds.
r-kahve.why: Judge the foam, then turn the cup over: the fal reading is the half of the ritual most visitors skip.
facts: Sade, az şekerli, orta or çok şekerli: sugar goes in before the boil, never after
