r-serpme.name: Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday
r-serpme.teaser: Twenty plates, three hours, and nothing else planned for the day. It is an appointment, not a breakfast
r-serpme.story: Serpme kahvaltı works as a booking, not a meal you drop into. On Sunday from about ten until two the breakfast houses hold tables rather than turn them, and you make one decision per person: the egg. Menemen soft-scrambled with tomato and green pepper, sahanda fried in the pan, sucuklu with cured sausage, or a plain omelette. Then the plates land together and keep landing: bal kaymak, buffalo cream under comb honey, bread replaced hot, at least one plate you cannot name, and çay refilled before you notice the glass is empty. The Turkish coffee comes last, never first.
r-serpme.why: Do it once, on a Sunday, with nothing after: it is the most time-expensive pleasure in this fold.
facts: 'Serpme kahvaltı' and the number of people: the count is heads, not plates
Sunday about 10:00–14:00 is the institution; go at nine or at three to miss the eleven o'clock crush
Book, or be at the door when it opens
Per head on the board, so read the number as what one of you pays; the same house on a weekday costs a fraction

r-raki-balik.name: Rakı-balık — choosing the fish off the ice
r-raki-balik.teaser: The fish is not on the menu. It is on ice by the door, priced by a kilo you have not yet asked about
r-raki-balik.story: The rakı table runs cold mezes, hot mezes, then one fish, and the fish is chosen, not ordered. You walk to the ice by the entrance, point, and it is weighed before it goes on the grill. That step is where visitors lose money most reliably in this city: the price is per kilo, the kilo price is often unposted, and a lüfer that looked like one dinner lands at nine hundred grams. Ask 'kilosu kaç?' before you point and ask to see the scale. Season decides the rest: palamut from September, lüfer peaking in October, hamsi through December.
r-raki-balik.why: Ask the kilo price before you point: a house that will not show it has already told you what it is.
facts: 'Kilosu kaç?' for the price per kilo; 'temizler misiniz?' to have it cleaned at a market counter
Fish in season; anything glossy and cheap in July is farmed or flown
Market counters in the morning, done by early afternoon; the rakı table in the evening, late

g-cinaralti.name: Çınaraltı, Çengelköy
g-cinaralti.teaser: Chairs set under a plane tree said to be nearly a thousand years old, on the Asian shore
g-cinaralti.story: The name means 'under the plane tree', and the tree is the whole proposition: a vast çınar on the Asian shore at Çengelköy, its canopy spread over tables that face the water. The garden pours tea and coffee and nothing else, and you are expected to bring your own food; people arrive with bags of it. There is no music, no backgammon, no nargile, and it keeps no closing hour. It is the least commercial room in this guide: you pay for the glass, and the shade and the Bosphorus come with it.
g-cinaralti.why: Bring a picnic and sit under the trunk: you pay for tea and nothing else.
facts: Tea and coffee only, by the glass
The near-thousand-year age of the tree is local telling, not a measured date

g-pierre-loti.name: Pierre Loti Kahvesi
g-pierre-loti.teaser: Tea on a hill above the graves, the whole Golden Horn laid out below, and a cable car to get up
g-pierre-loti.story: Evliya Çelebi knew this hill as the İdris Köşkü picnic ground. By the nineteenth century a coffeehouse called Rabia Kadın stood on it, and the French naval officer Julien Viaud, who wrote as Pierre Loti, arrived in 1876; he is said to have finished Aziyadé, published in 1879, at one of its tables. The hill took his name. Below the terrace lies Eyüp cemetery, long prized for its nearness to the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, over which Mehmed II raised a marble tomb and a mosque after 1453. Ride the cable car up; walk down through the graves.
g-pierre-loti.why: The descent on foot through the Ottoman cemetery is the reason to come, more than the tea.
facts: Teleferik from the Eyüp shore of the Golden Horn, about three minutes
Sunset, which is also the busiest
The walk back down through the cemetery
That Loti finished Aziyadé at this table is told, not documented

g-moda-aile.name: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi
g-moda-aile.teaser: The whole of Kadıköy, three generations of it, facing the Marmara over a backgammon board
g-moda-aile.story: A municipal tea garden on the slope above Moda's shore: umbrellas and plastic chairs under tall trees, the Sea of Marmara filling the view and the Princes' Islands on the horizon. Nobody here is performing. Grandparents, students and dog-walkers hold tables for hours over tea and tavla, the clatter of the pieces carrying between the trees, the food runs to sandwiches and toast, and half the room brought its own. This is what the Asian side does with a free afternoon, and on a clear evening the islands go blue and then dark while nobody moves.
g-moda-aile.why: Come late in the afternoon and stay through the sunset, at municipal prices with the Marmara in front of you.
facts: Caferağa, Park İçi Yolu, Moda, Kadıköy
Outdoor only, so the weather decides
Tea, with a sandwich or toast, or bring your own
The Princes' Islands on the horizon as the light goes

g-inci.name: İnci Pastanesi
g-inci.teaser: One dessert, one recipe, since the 1940s, and a redevelopment that moved the whole shop round the corner
g-inci.story: İnci opened in the Cercle d'Orient building on İstiklal in the mid-1940s and built its name on a single plate: the profiterol, choux balls filled with pastry cream under a pour of dark chocolate sauce. It is the version every other in the country is measured against. When the building was redeveloped in the early 2010s the shop was evicted, went dark for about seventy days, and reopened round the corner on Mis Sokak with the recipe unchanged. The room is new; the plate is the old one, and that is the only reason to come.
g-inci.why: Order the profiterol and nothing else: it is the benchmark for the whole country.
facts: The chocolate sauce: it is the recipe, more than the choux

g-markiz.name: Markiz (ex-Lebon)
g-markiz.teaser: Four Art Nouveau seasons were ordered from France; two of them are still on the wall
g-markiz.story: Lebon's patisserie traded on the Grand Rue from the 1880s and became the salon of Pera, with Pierre Loti and the poet Yahya Kemal among its regulars. Its Art Nouveau faience panels were ordered from France: four seasons were commissioned, and only Spring and Autumn hang in the room today. When Lebon moved across the street in 1940, Avedis Ohanyan Çakır opened Markiz in the space it left and kept the tiles. It closed in 1980 and came back, panels and all, in 2003. Take a table that faces the walls.
g-markiz.why: You pay grand-café prices to sit with the two surviving seasons of Pera's old salon.
facts: İstiklal Cad. 360–362, Beyoğlu, at the corner of the Oriental passage
The Spring and Autumn faience panels

g-kronotrop.name: Kronotrop, Cihangir
g-kronotrop.teaser: Sixteen and a half hours a day of table, on the Cihangir slope above Tophane
g-kronotrop.story: Kronotrop opened in 2012 as one of Turkey's first specialty roasteries; its founder, Çağatay Gülabioğlu, was the country's first Q grader. The Cihangir room is the flagship, on the slope above Tophane where many of the city's writers, editors and film people live, and it keeps the longest hours of any desk on this list, from seven in the morning to half past eleven at night. It is small and it fills, so the etiquette is one long session, not a whole day at the same table. The chain has passed forty branches with very different hours: aim for this one.
g-kronotrop.why: The early start and late close make it the one counter that fits round a crew's shifts.
facts: One long session, then give up the table
Beans roasted by the house, by the bag

g-montag.name: Montag Coffee Roasters
g-montag.teaser: The roaster most of the scene credits as the pioneer, and the Kadıköy room is where you sit
g-montag.story: Montag has roasted its own beans since 2016, and much of the city's specialty scene credits it as the pioneer. It runs rooms in Kadıköy, Moda and Bomonti, and the Kadıköy one on Muvakkıthane Caddesi is where you sit down: counter downstairs, a quiet upper floor, V60 and cold brew alongside espresso. The turnover is quick enough that the bag you buy was roasted recently, which matters if you are provisioning before a passage. The upstairs room is the working one, and Baylan sits at number 9 on the same street when you need a break.
g-montag.why: Buy beans here before a passage: the turnover keeps the bags fresh.
facts: Caferağa, Muvakkıthane Cad. No:16/A, first floor, Kadıköy
A V60 or cold brew, upstairs

g-petra.name: Petra Roasting Co., Bebek
g-petra.teaser: Where the shore walk ends and the morning's work starts, from half past seven
g-petra.story: The walk north from Arnavutköy along the water, past the wooden yalı, ends in Bebek, and Petra's Bebek branch opens at half past seven on weekdays: the obvious place to set a laptop down after the best early hour on the European shore. It is closed on Mondays, so build the walk around a Tuesday. If you are on the wrong side of the hill there are branches at Gayrettepe, Şişhane, Topağacı and Maslak; the Şişhane one also closes Mondays, the others do not. Weekends start later, at ten.
g-petra.why: Walk the shore from Arnavutköy first, then work here with the morning already done.
facts: The Arnavutköy to Bebek shore walk before it

g-ataturk.name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
g-ataturk.teaser: Eldem's 1970s library above Taksim: a research collection now, no longer an open reading room
g-ataturk.story: Sedad Hakkı Eldem, the architect who spent a career folding the Ottoman timber house into modernism, drew a culture complex here of library, museum and exhibition halls; only the library was built. Koç Holding raised it in 1973 and the collection moved in on 3 March 1981: around 228,000 books, 20,000 periodicals and 10,000 bound volumes of newspapers, with manuscripts, maps, albums and postcards. Since 5 September 2022 the city has run it as a research library: researchers are admitted, and general readers and students are sent to İBB's Sevgi Soysal library nearby. Come for the building and the archive, not a free desk.
g-ataturk.why: For a researcher, the city's Ottoman maps, albums and postcards under one Eldem roof.
facts: Gümüşsuyu, Miralay Şefikbey Sok. No:6, Beyoğlu
To researchers; hours not re-confirmed since the change, ask İBB before you go (Oct 2026)

g-salt.name: SALT Galata
g-salt.teaser: The Imperial Ottoman Bank's head office, emptied of money and handed to readers for nothing
g-salt.story: Alexandre Vallaury built this as the Imperial Ottoman Bank's headquarters, finished in 1892, and the bank worked from it until 1999. Han Tümertekin's conversion reopened it in November 2011 as SALT Galata: galleries, a street-level café and bookshop, and the bank's own archive covering 145 years. Reading costs nothing. The open library is for everyone; the Ferit F. Şahenk study hall takes registered researchers with a personal pass, in bookable blocks of up to three hours, and nothing circulates. Outside, the Camondo Stairs, cut around 1870 to 1880 by the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo, still climb the hill.
g-salt.why: A free, quiet desk inside a banking palace, with the Camondo Stairs a minute from the door.

g-yildiz.name: Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park
g-yildiz.teaser: A sultan's walled garden, two pavilions turned cafés, and a glass of çay under the trees
g-yildiz.story: Abdülhamid II walled the outer garden of Yıldız Palace and filled it with artificial lakes, summer houses and a porcelain factory that still works. Two of those pavilions, Çadır and Malta, now serve breakfast, lunch or a glass of tea under the trees, inside what has become a public park of some 368,000 square metres, run with the park's other restaurants by the municipal operator BELTUR. The honest work truth: the climb from the Beşiktaş gate is steep enough that nobody arrives wanting to open a laptop. Leave it on board and come for the trees.
g-yildiz.why: Come for the sultan's garden and a slow breakfast, not for a working day.

b-agora.name: Agora Meyhanesi 1890
b-agora.teaser: A Balat meyhane of 1890 where the rakı, not the clock, decides when dinner ends
b-agora.story: Agora suits a full rakı evening from the first cold meze to the last glass: about sixty mezes come off chef Ahmet Arı's counter, and the house is built for nights that do not stop at two hours. Go on a Thursday, book, and let the bottle set the pace.
b-agora.why: Book a Thursday and give it the whole evening; the counter rewards a slow table.

b-sofra.name: The rakı sofrası
b-sofra.teaser: Not a drink with dinner: a table that paces food across a whole evening
b-sofra.story: Under the Turkish Food Codex, rakı is suma, a grape or raisin distillate, redistilled with aniseed in copper pot stills of no more than 5,000 litres and bottled at 40 per cent or more. Add water and it clouds white: aslan sütü, lion's milk. The table keeps a fixed order. Cold mezes come first and stay a long time, then the hot ones, then the fish, while fasıl players move between tables. You drink at the speed of the table and never without food. Greeks, Armenians and Jews kept these houses for centuries; the authors were driven out in 1942, 1955 and 1964, and the form outlived them.
b-sofra.why: Order rakı and then slow down: eating fast beside it is the surest sign of a first visit.
facts: A Thursday table at any meyhane, with four hours set aside

b-stambouli.name: Lokanta Stambouli
b-stambouli.teaser: A Rum meyhane put back into Pera in late 2025, and by autumn 2026 nobody can say if it is still there
b-stambouli.story: Lokanta Stambouli opened in November 2025 on the first floor of Minoa Pera, the bookshop in the old Union Française building on Meşrutiyet Caddesi, and Gazete Oksijen wrote it up that month as a Turkish and Rum meyhane on the old Istanbul meze card. Perviz Resuli built it to work both traditions at once: lakerda and tarama on the cold counter, olive-oil cabbage dolma, cinnamon bean pilaki, then the day's fish. A Rum table back in Pera carries the history told in the rakı sofrası card. In August its own Instagram spoke of closing and moving, and no independent source has confirmed either way.
b-stambouli.why: If it is trading, go for the cold counter; if not, the empty first floor is part of the same story.

b-wayana.name: WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas
b-wayana.teaser: More than 500 Turkish labels, built to be poured a glass at a time, on a Moda side street
b-wayana.story: Moda, on a Kadıköy side street, and the most useful room in the city for anyone who thinks Turkish wine means a hotel Cabernet. By the house's own count in July 2026 the list holds more than 500 labels from 143 Turkish wineries and ninety endemic grape varieties, and it is meant to be poured by the glass. That changes the evening: you can taste eight native grapes in one sitting instead of gambling a whole bottle on one. Tapas come alongside, made to pair rather than to fill. Drink here first and the grape cards that follow read differently.
b-wayana.why: Ask for a flight of the rarest native grapes on the list; nowhere else lets you compare so many in a night.

b-solera.name: Solera Winery
b-solera.teaser: An all-Turkish list in a narrow Beyoğlu room, 300 metres off İstiklal, with its own Thracian vineyard
b-solera.story: Solera opened on 1 October 2011 on Yeni Çarşı Caddesi, 300 metres off İstiklal, and pours only Turkish producers: red, white, rosé, sparkling and fruit wine, with no imports on the card. Since 2013 the house has farmed its own vineyard at Gaziköy in Tekirdağ, on the Marmara shore of Thrace, and its Şarap Tadımı evenings walk a table through the country region by region. Watch the Thracian bottles, Chamlija's Papazkarası from the granite of the Strandja hills among them. The narrow room stays open late, and a cheese board or a plate of köfte will keep you there.
b-solera.why: Come on a Şarap Tadımı night: the region-by-region tasting is the fastest map of Turkish wine you will get.
facts: Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:44, Beyoğlu

b-sensus.name: Sensus Wine Boutique
b-sensus.teaser: A stone cellar in Kuledibi that buys its cheese as carefully as its wine
b-sensus.story: The stone cellar on Büyük Hendek Caddesi, a few steps below the tower in Galata, was the first Sensus; the business now runs thirteen shops across Türkiye, from Kavaklıdere in Ankara to Çeşme, Bursa and İzmir. Its buyers tour seven Turkish wine regions every quarter, buying direct from boutique producers, and the same trips bring back the cheese, charcuterie, honey, olives and oil on the counter. It is a shop that lets you sit down, not a bar with a shelf, so the pairing plate is the point. The retail price is the other reason to come: drink a glass, then carry the bottle out.
b-sensus.why: Taste here, then buy the bottle you liked at shop price for the boat.

b-okuzgozu.name: Öküzgözü & Boğazkere
b-okuzgozu.teaser: The bull's eye and the throat-scraper: Turkey's great red pairing, rarely poured apart
b-okuzgozu.story: Öküzgözü, 'bull's eye', comes from the villages around Elazığ and Malatya: violets, red and black plum, soft ripe tannin, medium-bodied and generous, and able to take oak without collapsing. Boğazkere grows down the Tigris around Diyarbakır and is its opposite, dense and structural with a tannic grip, the name meaning roughly 'throat-scraper'. Blended, the first sands down the second, and that blend is what Turkey exports as its own idea of red wine. Order each one alone once, to hear what it was contributing, and the blend makes sense afterwards.
b-okuzgozu.why: Taste them separately before the blend; it is the quickest way to understand eastern Anatolian red.
facts: Öküzgözü: violets, plum, soft tannin. Boğazkere: dense, dark, gripping

b-light-reds.name: Kalecik Karası, Papazkarası & Çalkarası
b-light-reds.teaser: Three grapes for the meze table: a near-lost Ankara red and two rosé grapes from opposite ends of Turkey
b-light-reds.story: Kalecik Karası grows at Kalecik, north-east of Ankara on the Kızılırmak, and was nearly lost: pale to medium, red cherry and strawberry, low tannin, the red Turkish drinkers describe by reaching for Gamay or Pinot Noir. Papazkarası, 'priest's black', is Thracian, thick-skinned and high in acid, now made as a varietal red, a blanc de noirs and a traditional-method sparkling. Çalkarası comes from Çal in Denizli and is best as rosé: pale, dry, sharp, tart cherry and pomegranate where Provence would give melon. All three are summer bottles, built for mezes rather than grilled meat, and still priced as curiosities.
b-light-reds.why: Order Kalecik Karası slightly cool with cold mezes, and a Çalkarası rosé when the fish arrives.
facts: Kalecik: red cherry, strawberry, light tannin. Papazkarası: bright acid. Çalkarası rosé: tart cherry and pomegranate

b-whites.name: Narince & Emir
b-whites.teaser: One name means 'delicately'; the other grape grows on Cappadocian volcanic rock
b-whites.story: Narince is Tokat's grape and its name means 'delicately': aromatic, medium to full-bodied, with a texture that carries oak without losing the fruit. Emir comes off the volcanic soils of Cappadocia and is its counterweight, high in acid, mineral and savoury, sharper and more austere, and the one of the pair with real ageing capacity. Between them they cover the whole Turkish white argument, and both cost very little set against any European equivalent. The rule of thumb at table is simple: Emir with fish and raw things, Narince with anything that comes out of a wood oven.
b-whites.why: Put Emir against raw fish and Narince against the wood oven, and the two grapes explain themselves.
facts: Narince: aromatic and rounded, happy with oak. Emir: high acid, mineral, savoury

b-mikla-bar.name: Mikla Bar
b-mikla-bar.teaser: The starred kitchen is upstairs; the terrace bar will pour you a drink without it
b-mikla-bar.story: Mikla's bar on the roof of The Marmara Pera runs separately from the tasting menu: take a stool or the terrace for the price of a cocktail and watch the old city skyline as the light goes.
b-mikla-bar.why: Come for one drink at the rail at dusk; the view is what you are paying for.

b-mezzepotamia.name: Roof Mezzepotamia
b-mezzepotamia.teaser: The roof English listings keep putting on the wrong shore, and the view that proves them wrong
b-mezzepotamia.story: Roof Mezzepotamia sits on the terrace of the Orient Occident Hotel in Sirkeci, on the historic peninsula, and not in Karaköy, where a run of English-language listings puts it. The mistake matters because the view runs the other way: from here you look back at Galata instead of out from it, across some 270 degrees of Bosphorus, Golden Horn and tower. The name folds mezze into Mesopotamia, and the kitchen works through the seven regions of Turkey. Sirkeci Station, terminus of the Orient Express from 1890, is a few doors away along the same streets.
b-mezzepotamia.why: Book the last of the light and watch the Galata Tower catch it across the Golden Horn.

b-before-roof.name: Before you go up
b-before-roof.teaser: On an Istanbul roof you are buying the sightline; the price, the hour and the season all follow from it
b-before-roof.story: Budget roughly TL 600 to 900 for a cocktail at a mainstream hotel roof, and TL 1,000 to 1,200 at the marquee Karaköy and Pera terraces, The Bank Roof Bar among them; the gap is the view, not the liquor, and both bands move with the lira. Turkey abolished daylight saving on 7 September 2016 and stays on UTC+3 all year, an hour ahead of its longitude, so summer light lasts very late. Arrive forty-five minutes early for a table on the rail. From about November to March many roofs glass in, cut hours or close, and listings lag behind.
b-before-roof.why: Phone on the day between November and March: a confirmed booking does not prove the roof is trading.

b-pera-palace.name: Pera Palace: Orient Bar & Kubbeli Saloon
b-pera-palace.teaser: The Orient Express hotel of 1895: its famous bar is dark, but the domed saloon still pours tea to piano
b-pera-palace.story: Alexandre Vallaury began the Pera Palace in 1892 and it opened in 1895 to lodge passengers off the Orient Express; it carried the first electric lift in Constantinople. The room people come for is the Orient Bar on the lobby floor, but the hotel's own page has kept it out of service until the end of the summer season, and nothing yet says it has reopened. The room that stays reliable is the Kubbeli, the domed saloon, where afternoon tea comes with live piano and the hotel names its pianist, Aslı Güral. Upstairs, Room 411 keeps Agatha Christie's books and a replica of her typewriter.
b-pera-palace.why: Take tea in the Kubbeli in daylight, and ask at reception whether Room 411 is free to look at.
facts: Kubbeli afternoon tea daily 15:00–18:00 (seen Aug 2026); Orient Bar out of service until the end of the summer season, per the hotel (Oct 2026)

b-ciragan.name: Le Fumoir & C Lounge, Çırağan Palace
b-ciragan.teaser: Four drinking rooms in an Ottoman palace on the strait, each with its own published dress code
b-ciragan.story: Çırağan was an imperial residence on the Bosphorus before it became a hotel, and its terrace sits on the water rather than above it. The Kempinski runs its drinking rooms as separate registers and publishes a code for each: Le Fumoir for the cigar-and-bar-snack end at smart casual, C Lounge as the casual bar, Çırağan Bar for refined spirits and cocktails at chic casual, and the Gazebo, the lobby lounge, an Ottoman-garden conceit with the strait in front of it. Tuğra, the palace's Turkish fine-dining room, is the formal end of the same building. Choose the room first, then dress for it.
b-ciragan.why: Pick the Gazebo for its garden and the water; check that room's code before you leave the boat.

b-flux.name: FLUX
b-flux.teaser: Funktion-One out in Maslak, where Friday and Saturday are deliberately not the same night
b-flux.story: FLUX is an RX Istanbul project in Maslak: a modular room that scales from fifty to five hundred people indoors, with a two-hundred-capacity terrace, all on Funktion-One. The split is deliberate. RX Fridaze runs house, groove-led and rhythmic; RX Saturdaze goes techno, deeper and harder. The opening season in autumn 2025 brought Ben Klock and Anja Schneider; the 2026 calendar carried Rødhåd, Regal, Tommy Four Seven, FJAAK in September and Answer Code Request later that month. Few floors in Istanbul take techno as seriously, and this one lies a long way north among the office towers, so budget for the taxi home.
b-flux.why: Choose the night by sound: Friday for house, Saturday for techno, and book the ride back before you go.

b-sahika.name: Şahika
b-sahika.teaser: Several floors above Nevizade, a roof on top, and the odd end of the programming
b-sahika.story: Şahika climbs several floors above the Nevizade lanes to a roof terrace, and it is where to go when four-to-the-floor is not what you want. Jungle and footwork share the bill with techno and house, local selectors play beside European guests, and exhibitions, talks and performances use the same building. It is queer-friendly by reputation and in practice, which in this city is a specific choice rather than a default. Friday nights listed on Resident Advisor through 2026 ran from 23:00 to past five in the morning. Start on the roof as the light fades and work downwards as it gets louder.
b-sahika.why: Climb up first and follow the volume down the stairs.

b-suma-han.name: Suma Han
b-suma-han.teaser: A Greek-built rakı distillery of 1923, now an artists' building with a club inside
b-suma-han.story: Suma Han was built in 1923 by the Greek architect Simotas and worked as a rakı distillation plant. It was bought in 2003, restored, and reopened in 2009 as offices, artist studios, residences and common rooms, with a club floor and real acoustics folded in: two stages, techno and psy-trance, plus exhibitions and talks. It is the city's clearest case of artists building their own infrastructure, and it stands inside a Greek-built rakı works a street back from the old Karaköy banks. The latest dated night found in October 2026 was from the previous autumn, so confirm a date before you go.
b-suma-han.why: Go for the building as much as the night: a rakı works turned into studios is its own argument.
facts: Bankalar Cad., Yanıkkapı Sok. No:3, Karaköy, Beyoğlu

n-arkaoda.name: Arkaoda
n-arkaoda.teaser: Kadıköy's anchor since 1999, and the rare Istanbul room that opened a branch in Berlin
n-arkaoda.story: Arkaoda opened on Kadife Sokak in 1999 and works more like a collective than a bar. Across a night the selectors move between Turkish psych, jazz and electronic, there is a garden out back, and the bookings lean towards independent artists nobody is paying to put on. Its Neukölln offshoot runs on the same principle, which makes this the rare Istanbul room that exported its idea rather than importing one. The doors open at midday and close at two in the morning, so you can begin an afternoon here with a coffee and still be in the garden after midnight.
n-arkaoda.why: Arrive in daylight for the garden and stay for the selectors once Kadife Sokak fills.
facts: Kadife Sok. No:18 D:1, Caferağa, Kadıköy

n-karga.name: Karga
n-karga.teaser: Five floors of an old wooden house and thirty years of Kadıköy's alternative scene, with a question mark
n-karga.story: Karga has traded since 1996 in a five-storey wooden house on Kadife Sokak, with KargART, its concerts, screenings and exhibitions, on the top two floors and vinyl sessions in the small rooms below. It is the building the Kadıköy alternative scene grew up inside. In August 2026 its own Facebook page carried a 'Closing Soon' notice; by October no press report of a closure had appeared and listings still showed it trading, so neither ending nor reprieve is confirmed. The programme lives on its Instagram rather than its website, which is a blank splash page, and that feed is the place to check.
n-karga.why: Check the feed on the day: if it is open, the vinyl rooms downstairs are the reason to climb in.
facts: A 'Closing Soon' notice on its own Facebook page (Aug 2026); no closure reported in the press (Oct 2026)

n-dama.name: Dama
n-dama.teaser: Filter coffee and laptops in the morning; vinyl through serious speakers once the light goes
n-dama.story: Dama sits on Şakayık Sokak in Teşvikiye and its own line is 'café by day, hi-fi by night'. Mornings are filter coffee, breakfast from nine and laptops on a quiet side street, with an open kitchen, ceramic surfaces and shelves of records. In the evening the same room turns into a hi-fi bar: vinyl through a system somebody clearly spent real money on, DJs, a short seasonal cocktail list built on things like macadamia and banana, and small plates. Istanbul has taken to the listening-bar format faster than most cities, and here you can watch the switch happen in one afternoon.
n-dama.why: Come late in the afternoon and stay through the changeover from coffee to records.
facts: Breakfast 09:00–13:00 weekdays, to 14:00 at weekends; hi-fi bar in the evening (seen Aug 2026)

n-kontra.name: Kontra Plak
n-kontra.teaser: An independent record shop on Yeni Çarşı since 2012, with a listening room attached
n-kontra.story: Kontra has traded since 2012 two doors from Galatasaray Lisesi, on the street that has quietly become Beyoğlu's record row. It carries new and second-hand Turkish and foreign vinyl, CDs, cassettes and music books, plus turntables, cartridges and headshells, and runs named strands rather than one-off events: Dinleme Odası, the listening room, Kontra'da, Örümcek and Just Kids, with in-store concerts each Record Store Day. Its weight shows against a loss: Lale Plak, on Galip Dede Caddesi since 1954, shut on 31 December 2019, and its owner Hakan Atala told Hürriyet it had been the musicians' meeting place.
n-kontra.why: Skip the reissue wall and dig the Turkish second-hand racks for 1970s Anadolu pressings.
facts: Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:60/A, Galatasaray, Beyoğlu

n-analog.name: Analog Kültür
n-analog.teaser: A record shop and studio on a Şahkulu cul-de-sac that will cut you a one-off record
n-analog.story: Analog Kültür opened on Record Store Day 2014, when the DJ and producer Kaan Düzarat went looking for somewhere to move his studio and decided it should be a record shop too; in late 2013, he said, there was nowhere in the city to find good electronic music, old or new. About eighty per cent of the stock is second-hand: seventies and eighties 45s, house, techno, drum and bass, krautrock, then jazz, funk, soul, bossa and Middle Eastern records. There is a proper hi-fi department, coffee, and, with Eazycut Records, lathe-cut records made to order.
n-analog.why: Bring a recording you love and ask about having it cut to vinyl.

n-akmar.name: Akmar Pasajı
n-akmar.teaser: The Kadıköy arcade that has been the city's second-hand book and record warren since 1982
n-akmar.story: Akmar stands on the site of the Özel Marmara Koleji, a school founded in 1957 whose building was damaged by construction next door in 1980, demolished, and replaced in 1982 by an office block with shops on the lower floors. The name is a splice of Akdik, the owning family's surname, and syllables of the school's. It runs through from Mühürdar Caddesi to Neşet Ömer Sokak, so half of Kadıköy uses it as a shortcut, and it holds a real place in the city's fanzine, metal and rock history. Second-hand booksellers dominate, with music shops among them.
n-akmar.why: Walk the whole passage slowly; the tenants turn over, the arcade does not.

n-nardis.name: Nardis Jazz Club
n-nardis.teaser: Istanbul's oldest dedicated jazz club, in an old Genoese building under the Galata Tower
n-nardis.story: Nardis opened in October 2002 in an old Genoese building on a side street by the Galata Tower, and Cornucopia calls it the oldest venue of its kind in the city. It is named after the Miles Davis tune and run by the guitarist Önder Focan, its art director, with Zuhal Focan, editor of the city's Jazz magazine. The room holds roughly 120 seats and books local and international acts nearly every night, with the programme already listed into the 2026–27 season. Wednesday is the night this guide plans around, when the room is full without being a scrum.
n-nardis.why: Book a Wednesday and sit close; the band plays a few metres from the tables.
facts: By email or phone through the club; online ticket sales ended (2025 listing)

n-cumhuriyet.name: Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi
n-cumhuriyet.teaser: A Balık Pazarı meyhane with live Turkish music every night and a table it keeps for Atatürk
n-cumhuriyet.story: The house has traded under its name since 1923, one street off the Beyoğlu fish market on Sahne Sokak, and by its own account Atatürk named it; take that as the family's claim, but the table it says he used is still kept permanently reserved. Turkish traditional live music is a standing nightly feature, not a weekend booking. The meze card keeps the old Istanbul minority repertoire most of Beyoğlu has quietly dropped: Armenian topik with caramelised onion and cinnamon, çiroz cut with dill and vinegar, kabak çiçeği dolması from Aegean flowers. Come late enough that the musicians are working the tables.
n-cumhuriyet.why: Order the topik and the çiroz, then stay until the fasıl reaches your table.

n-babylon.name: Babylon
n-babylon.teaser: The long-running live room in the old Bomonti brewery, booking jazz and left-field acts one night at a time
n-babylon.story: Babylon moved out of Beyoğlu into bomontiada, the old Bomonti brewery complex, in 2015, and did as much as anything to make the district a night out. Time Out Istanbul calls it the city's premier live venue, and the programme backs that up: jazz and left-field acts on single international nights rather than covers or residencies. In autumn 2026 the room carried the 36th Akbank Jazz Festival, with Yazmin Lacey and her band on 7 October, and the calendar also listed the Samora Pinderhughes Quintet and a Kelly Lee Owens DJ set. Its summer Soundgarden festival plays at Bonus Parkorman, not here.

p-kadikoy.name: Kadıköy market and the Tuesday pazar
p-kadikoy.teaser: Fish row and greengrocers five minutes up from the ferry, then the Tuesday pazar out at Hasanpaşa
p-kadikoy.story: Kadıköy's market is not a hall but a grid of short sloping streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, with Güneşlibahçe Sokağı as its spine: fishmongers at the bottom, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakers and a spice counter inside about eighty metres, and a butchers' row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the boats, not to a list. Commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so autumn brings palamut and lüfer, winter brings hamsi, and summer ice is mostly farmed levrek and çipura. On Tuesday the city's best-known pazar trades up at Hasanpaşa, ten minutes inland, where tomatoes go by the crate and herbs by the armful.
p-kadikoy.why: Do the street on a weekday morning, then walk inland on a Tuesday and stay for the pazar's last hour, when growers cut prices.

p-spice.name: Spice Bazaar and Hasırcılar Caddesi
p-spice.teaser: A 1660 hall built to pay for a mosque, and the back-gate street where its own traders buy
p-spice.story: Turhan Hatice Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, had the hall built as the rent-paying arm of the New Mosque; it was going up in the last months of 1660, after that July's great fire, and its name, Mısır Çarşısı, the Egyptian market, points at the province whose revenues paid for it. Eighty-five shops remain, and spice is retreating from them in favour of boxed lokum and pistachio pyramids built for photographs. Walk the L-shaped hall for the vault, then leave by the back gate onto Hasırcılar Caddesi, where roasters, nut merchants and cheese, pickle and pulse counters sell by the kilo, for less, to people who cook.
p-spice.why: Look inside, buy outside: pul biber, nar ekşisi, walnuts and grating cheese are cheaper on Hasırcılar for the same goods.

p-kadinlar.name: Kadınlar Pazarı
p-kadinlar.teaser: Siirt cheese, isot and comb honey under the Valens Aqueduct, still trading after the bazaars close
p-kadinlar.story: Below the arches of the Valens Aqueduct at Zeyrek, the streets were settled by families from Siirt and the south-east, and this market stocks what their kitchen needs: otlu peynir threaded with wild herbs, fat pistachios, isot, comb honey and dried pulses. Between the shops, büryan ovens are cut into the floor with lamb hanging in the pit; Siirt Şeref Büryan, which has its own table card, is the address for that. The hours are the surprise. OpenStreetMap has the shops working to 22:00 most days and 23:00 on Sunday, which makes this the one provisioning stop on the historic peninsula still lit when the bazaar quarters have shut.
p-kadinlar.why: Taste the otlu peynir before you buy: the herb should read as wild garlic and thyme, not salt with a green fleck.

p-besiktas-fish.name: Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı
p-besiktas-fish.teaser: The nearest serious fish counter to a Bosphorus berth, and no ferry ride with a cold box
p-besiktas-fish.story: Beşiktaş keeps its fish trade in the covered block behind the square, two minutes from the ferry, and unlike the Beyoğlu row it is still a market before it is a restaurant: whole fish on ice, chalked per kilo, gutted and scaled at the counter for nothing. Nut counters, helva makers and greengrocers close the list within a hundred metres. Learn the lüfer ladder before you point: çinekop, sarıkanat, lüfer and kofana are one fish at four ages, and Turkey sets a minimum landing size, so a stall pushing the smallest grade is telling you about itself. On Saturday a street pazar sets up north-west of the square.
p-besiktas-fish.why: Provision fish on the European shore without crossing the water: go mid-morning and say whether you want it scaled.

p-resat.name: Reşat Balık
p-resat.teaser: A fishmonger in the Beyoğlu Balık Pazarı since 1941, still cutting fish on a Sunday afternoon
p-resat.story: The house dates itself to 1941 and still runs its counter at Sahne Sokak 8, inside the Balık Pazarı off İstiklal, with a second one out at Bostancı on Bağdat Caddesi. Be clear about the setting: the old Beyoğlu fish market around it has thinned into meyhane tables and souvenir stalls, so the row is now more restaurant than market, and the counter is the only reason to walk in. What sets Reşat apart is the clock. OpenStreetMap has it open until 19:00 on Sunday, when most Istanbul fishmongers are done by lunch, and it is the closest serious fish counter to Pera and Galata.
p-resat.why: Your Sunday fish: the one counter near Galata still cutting after lunch, cleaned while you wait.

p-ferikoy.name: Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar
p-ferikoy.teaser: The Saturday growers' market where the residue results sit on a desk you can walk up to and read
p-ferikoy.story: Turkey's first ecological market opened on the Feriköy ground in June 2006, organised by the Buğday association, and by its fifteenth birthday it had grown to 330 stalls and 83 vendors. The model is a halk pazarı, growers selling direct, and certification rests on field visits and laboratory analyses. The thing to see is the public-relations stall, where inspection reports and residue results for what is on sale can be read on the spot. It was also the first market in the country to do away with plastic bags. The same covered yard hosts the Sunday antiques market, so check which day you have walked into.
p-ferikoy.why: Buy what city shops handle worst: raw honey, farm eggs, small-dairy butter and cheese, cold-pressed oils, unsprayed leaves.

p-kurukahveci.name: Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
p-kurukahveci.teaser: Coffee ground to order on Tahmis Sokak since 1871, handed over warm to a queue that never stops
p-kurukahveci.story: The house is in its 155th year and runs the anniversary as "155. YIL", and its counter is still at Tahmis Sokağı 66, at the corner of the Spice Bazaar, in the purpose-built block the company credits to the architect Zühtü Başar. It keeps only three shops of its own in the city: Eminönü, a Sirkeci branch, and Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 in Kadıköy. Everywhere else it is packaging. The queue is long and fast, and almost everyone in it buys one thing: Türk kahvesi, milled to order and passed over the counter still warm in its paper pack.
p-kurukahveci.why: Buy the smallest pack you will finish in a fortnight; it is ground cezve-fine and will choke an espresso basket.

p-namli.name: Namlı Gurme and the pastırma counter
p-namli.teaser: Pastırma cut thin enough to read through, at a Karaköy counter open every day from 07:00
p-namli.story: Pastırma comes from bastırma, to press: beef dried hard under çemen, a crust of crushed fenugreek, cumin, garlic and hot paprika, with Kayseri its centre since at least an 1893 British Foreign Office report. English took the word, as pastrami, by way of Yiddish. At Namlı's Karaköy counter it is sliced to order in front of you; ask for çemeni sıyrılmış, the crust scraped back, if you want the meat rather than the spice. The same counter carries kangal sucuk from the house workshop, Gelibolu and Kars eski kaşar, Erzincan tulum, Ayvalık olives, Makaron oil, tahin and Hakkari comb honey.
p-namli.why: One stop fills the cold store: vacuum-packed pastırma and sucuk keep for weeks chilled, and the counter never takes a day off.

f-lale.teaser: Tripe soup against the last rakı, ladled at any hour on Tarlabaşı Bulvarı since 1960
f-lale.story: When the meyhane lights go off, the Beyoğlu night ends here with a bowl of işkembe dressed at the table with garlic vinegar and lemon. It does not shut: the house claims 24 hours, seven days a week.

f-kizilkayalar.name: Kızılkayalar
f-kizilkayalar.teaser: The ıslak burger sweating in its steam case on the Taksim corner: the city's agreed last bite
f-kizilkayalar.story: At 03:00 on the Sıraselviler corner of Taksim the steam case is still glowing, and the ıslak hamburger, small, garlicky and soaked in tomato sauce, is how the city ends a night. It publishes no closing hour; the after-midnight queue is the institution.

f-gulluoglu.name: Karaköy Güllüoğlu and the Güllü split
f-gulluoglu.teaser: Pistachio baklava from the one Karaköy shop, still cutting trays after the bars go quiet
f-gulluoglu.story: Baklava reached Gaziantep in 1871 with Çelebi Güllü, who had learned it from a chef in Damascus, and in 2013 Antep Baklavası became the first Turkish product to win an EU protected geographical indication. The family grew and divided. Nadir Güllü, fifth generation, runs the single Karaköy shop at Kemankeş Caddesi 67, and the house dates itself to 1843. The largest holder of the name, Faruk Güllü, has dropped Güllüoğlu from its signs and trades through many branches from a Büyükçekmece plant. Read the first name, not the surname: a Güllüoğlu counter in a mall or an airport is neither of the two.
f-gulluoglu.why: Order fıstıklı kuru by weight: the dry pistachio cut, no cream, is the one that survives the walk back to the boat.

f-haci-bekir.name: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir
f-haci-bekir.teaser: Lokum cut from the tray at the city's oldest sugar counter, and an invention claim nobody can prove
f-haci-bekir.story: By the house's account the founder came down from Kastamonu and opened at Bahçekapı in 1777; three generations served as Şekerci Başı, head confectioner to the palace, and five have kept the shop, which grew to 88 square metres by swallowing the spice shop next door. Lokum itself is a gel of starch and sugar scented with rosewater, mastic, bergamot or lemon. Hacı Bekir is often credited with inventing it, but the Oxford Companion to Food says there is no real evidence, and Persian starch-and-sugar recipes are centuries older. Walk past the lokum to the second counter: akide şekeri, the hard palace candy the house made first.
f-haci-bekir.why: Ask for sakızlı and gül cut from the tray, never a sealed box.

f-saray.name: Saray Muhallebicisi
f-saray.teaser: Chicken in the milk pudding and a scorched pan bottom: what a muhallebici makes and a patisserie cannot
f-saray.story: Hüseyin Topbaş opened in Kasımpaşa in 1935 with an aim the company still prints: to feed the elegant ladies and gentlemen of Beyoğlu the finest desserts. It took until 1949 to move onto İstiklal, and that room is the one with the history; the other branches, 21 by the house's own count, are the chain it paid for. Order what the trade exists for. Tavuk göğsü is milk pudding thickened with chicken breast pounded to threads until you cannot find it; kazandibi is the same pudding scorched on the pan bottom and turned out caramel side up. At breakfast, bal kaymak with fresh bread heads the house's own list.
f-saray.why: Order tavuk göğsü once, so you can say you ate chicken for dessert and never noticed.

f-vefa.name: Vefa Bozacısı
f-vefa.teaser: Thick, pale, faintly sour boza, poured at one Vefa counter since September 1876
f-vefa.story: Hacı Sadık Bey came from Prizren in 1870 and spent six winters carrying boza through the streets in copper vessels before opening here in September 1876, in what the house calls the first registered boza shop in the world. He fixed the style the city still expects: thick-bodied, pale yellow, caught as the fermentation bubbles first rise, only lightly sour. His son İsmail Hakkı followed him, the fourth generation runs it now, and vinegars, grape şıra and şerbet carry the shop through summer. Drink it standing, dusted with cinnamon, roasted leblebi to chew alongside, near the glass said to have been used by Atatürk.
f-vefa.why: Come between October and April, when boza is what the shop is for; in August you are buying vinegar.

f-kunefe.name: Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası
f-kunefe.teaser: Antakya künefe from the copper dish, eaten in the minute while the cheese still pulls
f-kunefe.story: The house came north from Hatay, and the reason to end a meal here is the region's dessert: shredded kadayıf packed round fresh, unsalted, unaged cheese, baked in a shallow copper dish until both faces are dark, then drowned in syrup at the pass. It is only itself while the cheese still pulls, and it dies within minutes of leaving the copper, so order it at the end and eat it the moment it lands. The İstiklal room faces the French Consulate, but OpenStreetMap puts the door just behind the avenue on Meşelik Sokağı, so expect to turn the corner. A second room is out at Etiler.
f-kunefe.why: One künefe shared after a full Hatay table is plenty; never take it away.

f-mado.name: Mado and kesme dondurma
f-mado.teaser: Kahramanmaraş ice cream stiff enough for knife and fork, at any decent branch
f-mado.story: The company traces it to snow carried down from Ahır Dağı above Kahramanmaraş and enriched with milk, honey and salep. Yaşar Kanbur began by selling ice cream from a small shop beside the Aras bus garage; the family built a Kahramanmaraş factory in 1965, brought in machines in 1970 and modernised properly in 1989. Two ingredients do the work: goat milk, from the company's own farm, and salep, the ground orchid tuber that makes the ice cream stretch and refuse to melt. Demand has thinned the region's wild orchids enough that Turkey banned salep export. With several hundred branches, it is a reference point, not a pilgrimage.
f-mado.why: Ask for kesme dondurma sade, the plain slab, so goat milk and salep are the whole flavour; the cone is the tourist version.

f-baylan.name: Baylan Pastanesi
f-baylan.teaser: The republic's oldest pâtisserie, and the ice-cream coupe Harry Lenas invented there in 1954
f-baylan.story: Filip Lenas, a Greek of Albanian origin, opened in 1923 with his cousin Yorgi Kiriçi in Deva Çıkmazı, as Loryan, the Turkish ear's version of Le Orient, and moved onto İstiklal in 1928. The Kadıköy shop most people now mean by Baylan was opened by Mikail Lenas in 1961. Its own invention is the Kup Griye, created by Harry Lenas in 1954: vanilla and caramel ice cream under whipped cream, honeyed almonds and caramel sauce, a kedidili biscuit on the side. Altınmarka, owner of Kahve Dünyası, bought the business in 2009 and has kept opening rooms, at Galataport in 2021 and Kız Kulesi in 2024.
f-baylan.why: Take a table at the Kadıköy shop and order the Kup Griye by name; it is the one thing you cannot get anywhere else.
facts: Hacı Bekir's Kadıköy counter, four doors along the same street

v-yemek.name: Yemek ve Kültür
v-yemek.teaser: The scholarly food journal that grew out of a Kadıköy kebab shop, four issues a year in print only
v-yemek.story: The first issue appeared in January 2005 from Çiya, the house behind Çiya Sofrası, and it has come out four times a year since, in print only. Zeynep Dağdeviren is the responsible editor and Musa Dağdeviren sits on the board, filing seven forgotten folk recipes in every issue. The advisory board includes Evangelia Balta, the historian of the Turkish-speaking Ottoman Orthodox Christians, which tells you how seriously the journal takes the question of who actually cooked this food. Issue 84 was the current one in August 2026, and the subscription delivers inside Turkey only, so a copy is something to carry home.
v-yemek.why: Read it for the recipes nobody else has written down: seven forgotten ones every issue, from Musa Dağdeviren.
facts: Quarterly print journal of food history and folk recipes, since January 2005

v-milor.name: Vedat Milor
v-milor.teaser: A Berkeley sociologist who became the country's most argued-with palate
v-milor.story: Born in 1955, Vedat Milor went through Galatasaray Lisesi, read economics at Boğaziçi, took a master's at the LSE and a doctorate in sociology at Berkeley, where his thesis was named the best of 1990 by the American Sociological Association. He then turned that apparatus on restaurants, first in the newspaper Milliyet and then in a long-running programme on NTV, and he now edits the English-language Gastromondiale. In Istanbul his verdict moves a booking sheet the way a star does, which is reason enough to know what he has said about a room before you sit down in it.
v-milor.why: Check his take before a big booking: a Milor verdict changes who can get a table.
facts: Restaurant critic and broadcaster; editor of Gastromondiale

v-oney.name: Aylin Öney Tan
v-oney.teaser: The one Turkish food writer still filing a weekly column in English
v-oney.story: Trained as an architect and once project manager on the World Bank's cultural heritage project in Turkey, Aylin Öney Tan writes on food for Hürriyet Daily News, the country's oldest English-language daily, and in Turkish for Cumhuriyet. The column is current rather than archival: she was filing through July 2026, on gastronomic diplomacy at state dinners, on the Culture Route Festival mapping fifty taste stops across Bursa, and on the seasonal logic Istanbul kitchens actually work to. For anyone without Turkish, it is the best way into Anatolian regional food, written by someone who has eaten her way across it.
v-oney.why: Read a month of her columns before you arrive and you will know what is in season when you land.

v-cb.name: Culinary Backstreets
v-cb.teaser: Two men in Istanbul writing up lunch, and they never lost the habit
v-cb.story: It began as Istanbul Eats, a blog run by Ansel Mullins, who worked in historic restoration, and Yigal Schleifer, then the Christian Science Monitor's Istanbul correspondent; the site first shows up in the web archive in April 2009. It has since grown into food tours and reporting across close to thirty cities, but Istanbul is still the deepest desk, with a city guide, regular dispatches and walking tours, and the old istanbuleats.com address now simply redirects here. The writing is about who cooks, where they came from and what the lunch counter down the street is doing this year.
v-cb.why: Search its Istanbul archive by neighbourhood before you walk one; the lunch counters it lists are the ones locals use.
facts: Food reporting, city guides and walking tours, with Istanbul as its deepest desk

v-cornucopia.name: Cornucopia
v-cornucopia.teaser: For people who came for the food and stayed for the Ottoman archive
v-cornucopia.story: Launched in 1992 and made between Scotland, London and Turkey, Cornucopia publishes two issues a year at a circulation above twenty thousand, edited by John Scott with Berrin Torolsan as publishing director. Its register is connoisseurial: architecture, textiles, gardens, Anatolian archaeology, and food treated as material culture rather than as a booking problem. A piece on a palace kitchen or a Bosphorus yalı will tell you more about what was eaten there than any menu. The complete digital archive of every issue comes with a subscription of about nineteen pounds a year, which is the real reason to sign up.
v-cornucopia.why: Buy the digital archive and search it for the place you are about to see.
facts: Biannual magazine on Turkish art, architecture, history and food, since 1992
cornucopia.net; print and digital; digital subscription about GBP 19 a year (seen Aug 2026)

v-recap.name: Turkey recap
v-recap.teaser: Why the bar you loved is suddenly not serving alcohol
v-recap.story: Turkey recap started as an English-language newsletter in October 2019, written by journalists based in Istanbul and Ankara; Diego Cupolo co-founded it with Raziye Akkoç. It is independent and reader-supported, published since 2023 by Kolektif Medya Derneği, an Istanbul non-profit, with one weekly letter on politics and foreign affairs and another on business and the economy, plus a Turkish-language strand. It is not a food publication, but licensing, alcohol regulation, inflation and the lira set what an Istanbul evening costs and whether the meyhane down the road can still pour, and this is where those changes get explained first.
v-recap.why: Subscribe for the month you are in the city: it explains the price and licensing shifts before the bill does.
facts: Independent news newsletter on Turkish politics and economy, two letters a week
turkeyrecap.com; paid, with a free trial

v-ohp.name: Ottoman History Podcast
v-ohp.teaser: Academics talking properly, without the academic gate
v-ohp.story: It started in March 2011 as an experiment in accessible scholarly production and became one of the largest digital resources of its kind on the Ottoman Empire and the modern Middle East. Chris Gratien, now at the University of Virginia, has recorded more than two hundred interviews with historians, and the project carries no advertising and takes no revenue. A parallel Turkish-language strand runs alongside the English one. For a cook or a guest heading for Istanbul, the archive has whole episodes on coffee, wine, famine and the millet system, each one a better primer than a guidebook chapter.
v-ohp.why: Search the archive for coffee and wine before the trip; the episodes change what you notice in the Spice Bazaar.
facts: Free scholarly podcast on Ottoman and modern Middle Eastern history, since March 2011

v-iksv.name: İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts
v-iksv.teaser: One foundation programmes most of the big weeks in the Istanbul year
v-iksv.story: İKSV runs the Istanbul Film Festival, the Music Festival, the Jazz Festival, the Theatre Festival, the Istanbul Biennial and the Design Biennial, plus Filmekimi and the year-round Salon İKSV stage, and it curates the Turkish Pavilion at the Venice Biennale. That makes its calendar the single page that tells you which week the city's halls, hotels and best tables will be full of festival crowds. Check it against your dates before you fix a dinner: a jazz night or a biennial opening may be worth moving a booking for, and a sold-out week is worth knowing about early.
v-iksv.why: Check the calendar against your dates before you book a single table.
facts: The foundation behind Istanbul's film, music, jazz and theatre festivals and the Biennial

v-timeout.name: Time Out Istanbul
v-timeout.teaser: The English backstop when you need something open tonight
v-timeout.story: Time Out runs a full local Istanbul edition in English and in Turkish, across restaurants and cafes, things to do, film, music and nightlife, art and culture. It is a commercial listings operation, not a critical guide, and it should never settle an argument about where to eat. Where it earns its place is the practical layer: opening hours, one-off events and whatever has just opened in the street you are standing in. Its listings are often the only English record of a shop's hours, though many are undated, so treat a time there as a lead to confirm rather than a promise.
v-timeout.why: Use it for tonight's hours and events, then confirm by phone; never for the verdict on a meal.
facts: Commercial listings guide to the city's food, events and nightlife
